paper_content.abstract: Photodiodes are central to high-speed communication, sensing and light-harvesting devices. While silicon and other inorganic semiconductor-based photodiodes have been widely integrated into commercial technologies, photodiodes from excitonic semiconductors continue to maintain high interest in research. Excitonic semiconductors are superior in terms of absorption as compared to silicon and III-V semiconductors, but have always suffered from poor charge transport and narrowband absorption due to the short diffusion lengths and resonant nature of the excitons, respectively. Here, we attempt to solve both these central issues in excitonic photodiode devices via use of polariton physics and demonstrating photodiodes in the strong light-matter coupling regime. By using a conductive tin-doped indium oxide transparent top electrode that also serves as an anti-reflective coating combined with self-trapping and hybridization of light in inorganic excitonic semiconductor WS2, we demonstrate photodiodes with broadband absorption and internal quantum efficiency values approaching unity near the zero-detuning condition. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the response speed of photodiodes is enhanced under strong coupling. Our work presents a promising approach to explore the physics and applications of photodiodes based on excitonic semiconductors.
paper_content.introduction:
Photodiodes and photovoltaics based on excitonic semiconductors have emerged as a potentially low-cost alternative to conventional semiconductors1–9, owing to their markedly enhanced absorption coefficients in photon harvesting processes10–12. In excitonic photodiodes and photovoltaics (e.g., organic photovoltaics), the excited state (exciton) must diffuse to a heterointerface before being separated into free carriers13–15. However, poor exciton transport is often a limiting factor on device efficiency.

Strong coupling between excitons and cavity photons can occur by placing an excitonic material into an optical cavity with a discrete mode in resonance with the exciton energy16–21. The resulting hybrid states are called exciton-polaritons (EPs). EPs, in contrast to excitons, can exhibit long-range transport due to a low effective mass and delocalized wavefunction22–27. Recently, the utilization of strong coupling in organic semiconductor devices has been demonstrated, leading to longer exciton diffusion lengths and enhanced photocurrent28–33. Notably, most of the previously reported studies on organic photovoltaic devices have required external optical cavities for strong light-matter interactions due to the low refractive indices, thus resulting in considerable energy loss from partially transparent metal top reflectors, leading to the inability to obtain state-of-the-art device performance. In contrast, recent advances in open-cavity architectures have demonstrated a viable pathway toward substantial absorption enhancement without such trade-offs34,35.

Two-dimensional (2D) transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) feature dielectric screening and strong confinement effects that lead to unusually large exciton binding energies in monolayers (>300 meV), but their van der Waals bonding out of plane also ensures binding energies >25 meV in the bulk. Thus, exciton photophysics governs photoexcited carriers at room temperature36. Furthermore, the large optical constants and strong light-matter interactions enable strong light absorption in the films37–39. TMDCs of Mo and/or W, in particular, show simultaneously strong exciton resonances and large optical constants, enabling self-hybridized EPs and providing a natural platform for investigating photon-exciton coupling without the need for external optical cavities40–42.

Here, we demonstrate a self-hybridized exciton-polariton photodiode with a transparent conductive top electrode also acting as an antireflective coating, enabling strong light-matter coupling with broadband light absorption and polariton-enhanced transport. The strong-coupling effect is observed with large polariton peaks and dispersion behavior in thickness-dependent reflectance spectra. Corresponding polariton peaks are also observed from external quantum efficiency (EQE) spectra, indicating that the EP states enhance the generation of photocurrent. The strong coupling of excitons to cavity photons in the WS2 absorber layer enhances the internal quantum efficiency (IQE) to near unity. The exciton polariton transport achieved improves the response speed of the diode, obtaining the fastest response time of 217 ns. This work demonstrates that strong light-matter coupling in self-hybridized structures can be used to design polaritonic photodiodes with broadband absorption and polariton-enhanced transport for improved quantum efficiency and response speed.
paper_content.results:
Device structure and working principle
The exciton-polariton photodiode is shown in Fig. 1a. WS2 is contacted by a tin-doped indium oxide (ITO) layer that functions as both an electrode and an anti-reflective coating layer. The thickness of the WS2 active layer varies from 5 nm to 200 nm. The index contrast between ITO and air enables the ITO to be used as an antireflective coating (ARC). However, the large optical impedance mismatch between the ITO and WS2 results in a Fresnel reflection coefficient at the interface that can produce Fabry-Perot (FP) cavity modes in the WS2 layer. The energy of the FP cavity modes depends approximately linearly on the WS2 thickness, and dipole-dipole interactions between the cavity photons and the WS2 excitons result in self-hybridized EPs for WS2 layers of appropriate thicknesses. Therefore, our ITO/WS2 devices can simultaneously exhibit self-hybridized EPs and strong off-resonance absorption, benefiting from the ARC and high imaginary permittivity of WS2 above its bandgap.

A representative device optical image and corresponding photocurrent map illustrate that the photocurrents are spatially distributed uniformly over the entire device range. (Fig. 1b, Supplementary Fig. 1). Generally, the transport of energy carriers in solid state materials is determined by their wave function and their interaction with the environment. As shown in Fig. 1c, conventional photodiodes suffer from three primary energy loss mechanisms: i) the photon with energy E < Eg cannot be absorbed by the material; ii) additional kinetic energy loss of the electron-hole pairs; and iii) recombination of electron-hole pairs. These losses stem mainly from poor charge transport and limited bandgap absorption. In contrast, EPs as neutral bosonic quasiparticles can substantially suppress the Coulomb scattering that plagues conventional charge carriers43. This suppression leads to longer diffusion lengths and lowers scattering rates, thereby opening avenues for enhanced exciton transport and improved overall photoelectric conversion efficiency44–47. In exciton-polariton photodiodes, absorption occurs through exciton-polariton states, the physical nature of which can be revealed by the wavefunction properties: the polariton wavefunction can be described as a linear superposition of photon and matter excitations48,49. This particular quantum superposition state determines the way energy is distributed in the light-matter system and the energy transport process. Specifically, the exciton-polariton state causes oscillations between photons and excitons at the Rabi frequency, i.e., photons are periodically absorbed and re-emitted through the exciton state. Under strong coupling conditions, the effective mass, and therefore the transport, is mainly determined by the photon composition, and the excitons are able to achieve transport through photonic modes, so that exciton transport can be improved to exhibit longer diffusion lengths. The hypothesized principle of photocurrent generation is similar to that of pure exciton photovoltaic devices, i.e., the exciton dissociates into a free charge at the interface, but in strong coupling, the exciton is transported in a photon-like mode and dissociates at the charge-selective contact, one charge being immediately extracted while the opposite free charge undergoes drift-diffusion transport to the other contact. In this study, we leverage the strong absorption and low effective mass of EPs to enhance the performance of photodiodes. In Fig. 1d, we schematically elucidate the relationship between the emergence of multiple polariton branches in the WS2 strong coupling device. The exciton-polariton states can enhance the subgap photon absorption and exciton diffusion length, which can minimize the energy loss and improve the quantum efficiency. While the presence of polaritons in our devices is clearly evidenced by enhanced absorption and spectral quantum efficiency, the overall photodetector performance, particularly the response speed, remains below the theoretical polaritonic limits owing to material and interface imperfections. Interfacial trap states induce nonradiative recombination and hinder carrier extraction, while non-ideal contact geometry may further constrain carrier collection dynamics. Importantly, these are technological rather than fundamental limitations. Advancing crystal and interface quality (e.g., through improved encapsulation and transfer processes), optimizing dielectric environments, and especially implementing carefully designed integrated cavities with higher Q factors and tighter mode confinement could substantially enhance the light-matter coupling strength and absorption efficiency. Together with refined electrode configurations for rapid carrier extraction, these improvements could bridge the gap toward the theoretical performance limits of polaritonic photodetectors.

Strong coupling in self-hybridized polaritonic photodiodes
We performed thickness-dependent reflectance measurements, transfer matrix method (TMM) calculations, and fitting to the coupled oscillator model to confirm the presence of strong coupling in our devices50. Figure 2a shows the TMM-calculated thickness and wavelength-dependent reflectance of our devices. Polaritons appear in the calculated reflectance spectra as reflectance minima that exhibit anti-crossing behavior near the exciton resonance (approximately 1.97 eV for WS2, denoted by the yellow vertical dotted lines in Fig. 2a, b). For each cavity mode order, the dispersion is fit with the coupled oscillator model, in which we include decay of the exciton and cavity modes22,51. The resulting fit is overlaid in Fig. 2a as dashed white lines, and the corresponding bare cavity modes are overlaid as red dashed lines. The Rabi splitting values between the upper and lower polariton branches (UPB and LPB) for the first 3 FP cavity modes (l=1, 2, 3) are found to be ℏΩ = 152.62 meV (l=1), 173.38 meV (l=2), and 171.42 meV (l=3), respectively (Supplementary Fig. 3). The real values of Rabi splitting confirm that the devices are in the strong coupling regime when thicknesses support cavity modes with resonances near the A exciton. For thicknesses below approximately 50 nm, the devices are in the weak coupling regime, as evidenced by the asymmetric Fano resonances slightly blueshifted from the exciton resonance52.

Figure 2b shows experimentally measured and reflectance spectra for representative devices of varying thickness. The corresponding TMM calculations (dashed black lines) match the measured spectra very well. The dispersion of the UPB and LPB is shown by the purple dotted lines. Spectra are offset vertically for clarity. Notably, the absorbance is large and broadband, and the polariton branches can be seen to extend the spectral range of absorption while exhibiting near unity absorption. To further resolve weak or overlapping features, we performed derivative analysis of the measured spectra (Supplementary Fig. 5)53. The first derivatives (Supplementary Fig. 5b) highlight inflection points corresponding to reflectance extrema, revealing subtle spectral features otherwise obscured in the raw data. Representative derivative spectra (Supplementary Fig. 5c) for devices in the strong-coupling regime (151.2 nm, 77.3 nm) display two well-resolved peaks straddling the A-exciton energy, fully consistent with the formation of UPB and LPB. Angle-resolved reflectivity spectra of devices with different thicknesses further reveal the coupling regime. Pronounced anti-crossing features were observed for WS2 layers thicker than 50 nm, consistent with strong exciton-photon hybridization, while thinner devices displayed only a dispersionless excitonic resonance. Coupled oscillator model fits quantitatively reproduce the experimental dispersions and confirm strong coupling across representative thicknesses (see Supplementary Fig. 6, Table 1). More detailed information on the simulation method is provided in the Supplementary Fig. 3 section.

EQE spectra driven by exciton-polariton states
We now consider the spectral response of WS2 photodiodes operating in the strong coupling regime. EQE is an important metric for photodiodes and photovoltaics as it reflects the ratio of the charge carrier flux (i.e., current density) collected at the electrodes to the incident photon flux at a specific excitation wavelength. EQE measurements (“methods”) are performed in the 500 nm to 800 nm range on devices with WS2 thicknesses from 17 to 200 nm (Supplementary Fig. 9). To accurately identify the polariton-related photocurrent features, we performed first-derivative analysis of the EQE spectra (Supplementary Fig. 9b, c). This method sharpens spectral features and pinpoints inflection points that correspond to EQE maxima. Figure 2c shows the coupled oscillator model fit, along with the experimental EQE peak wavelengths extracted from a range of device thicknesses (Supplementary Fig. 9b). Notably, the peak response positions of the EQE spectra in devices with varying thicknesses (scattered dots) exhibit excellent agreement with the theoretical model (dashed lines). In particular, the evolution of their wavelength positions with thickness strictly follows the characteristic dispersion relation of polaritons, with the peak positions corresponding to the resonance modes of the UP and LP branches, respectively. This consistency between experimental observations and the theoretical model provides solid evidence that the polariton state enhances light-trapping efficiency by modulating photon-exciton interactions, clearly demonstrating the crucial role of polariton engineering in improving photodiode performance. Figure 2d shows the EQE spectra of three representative devices, one in the weak coupling regime, one near zero detuning for the first-order polariton, and one near zero detuning for the second-order polariton. In these strongly coupled devices, both the UPB and LPB exhibit spectral separations from the bare exciton resonance that exceed their respective linewidths. This clear spectral separation enables unambiguous identification of the polariton branches. The responses below the bare exciton energy of the strongly coupled devices can be observed, and the peaks of the responses correspond to the reflectance minima (attributed to UP and LP branches) reported in the previous section (Fig. 2b). These features are absent in weakly coupled devices, confirming that all these responses are dominated by the exciton-polariton states. Based on this, we can predict that the strong-coupling device can harvest more photons in the spectral region around the bandgap due to the formation of exciton-polariton states.

Further, we note that the response of the photodiodes is broadband, highlighting the benefit of the ITO ARC. Simultaneously, the cut-off wavelength of the device is extended (Supplementary Fig. 11).

Compared with conventional excitonic materials, the narrow-band absorption properties due to the strong exciton binding effect and the ability to achieve high absorption efficiency only at specific wavelengths are avoided.

In addition, to further explore whether the exciton properties are preserved during the transport process and the effect of polariton coupling on quantum efficiency, we performed reflectance spectra, I–V characteristics, and EQE spectra measurements at low temperatures (Fig. 2e, f, Supplementary Figs. 12, 13). The results show that:
i) A comparison of the I-V curves at 300 K and 80 K reveals a significant reduction in dark current, attributed to the decreased concentration of thermally excited carriers, indicating a lower density of free carriers at low temperatures.
ii) In both strong- and weak-coupling devices, we observe a pronounced steepening of the exciton absorption edges, a blue shift of the absorption maxima, and an enhancement of the EQE at low temperatures under both resonant and non-resonant excitation, reflecting the strengthened excitonic and polaritonic effects. Such enhancement may also partially arise from polariton-mediated modification of radiative rates (Purcell-like effect)54, suggesting a direction for future studies to quantitatively evaluate this effect. Correspondingly, the absorption peaks dominated by the UPB and LPB are also clearly resolved in the EQE spectra, as indicated by the black arrows in Fig. 2f. To capture the full thermal evolution of these coupled states, we carried out continuous temperature-dependent reflectance spectra from 87 K to 300 K on WS2 cavities with thicknesses ranging from ∼35 nm to ∼130 nm. Across all devices, the UPB and LPB display a smooth, monotonic redshift with increasing temperature. Importantly, the polariton branches remain spectrally resolved over the entire temperature range without collapsing into a single peak, confirming that the system persistently resides in the strong-coupling regime. The temperature-induced evolution of the spectral splitting is accompanied by consistent trends in the EQE spectra, with devices near zero detuning exhibiting distinct peak splitting even at elevated temperatures. These observations substantiate the assignment of the observed features to robust exciton-photon hybrid states (polaritons), rather than to uncoupled optical modes or interference fringes.

Based on these observations, we speculate that at low temperatures, the EQE is predominantly dominated by exciton and polariton contributions, owing to the preservation and enhancement of exciton and polariton properties of WS2 and the suppression of the free-carrier effect. This further demonstrates that polaritons contribute to photovoltaic conversion and could potentially be exploited to enhance exciton transport and improve the photonic energy conversion efficiency of excitonic semiconductors.

External and internal quantum efficiency
To quantify the effect of strong coupling on the overall photoelectric conversion efficiency and the internal processes of the WS2 devices, we calculated the EQE and the IQE of the devices as a function of thickness for wavelengths of 600 nm, 630 nm, and 650 nm (Fig. 3). To eliminate uncertainty, at each thickness, we prepared multiple devices with similar thicknesses (≥3) and performed multiple measurements (≥5), then extracted the mean and standard deviation. The EQE reflects both the absorption and internal excitation-to-charge collection processes in the device. It is known that polaritons enhance absorption on resonance and can extend the spectral responsivity of photodiodes through absorption in the LPB. Polaritons are also expected to improve carrier extraction due to improved exciton diffusion. The greatest hybridization (i.e. strongest coupling) between photons and excitons occurs when there is zero detuning between the photonic mode and the exciton energy. In our devices, this occurs at WS2 thicknesses of approximately 75 nm for the first FP cavity mode and 145 nm for the second FP cavity mode. Consequently, we see oscillatory behavior in the EQE with thickness, with peaks near the first and second zero detuning thicknesses, evidencing the beneficial effects of strong coupling. In addition to the oscillatory behavior, there is a drastic increase in EQE for all wavelengths as the thickness enters the strong coupling regime. The increase in EQE from the weak coupling regime to the strong coupling regime is a factor of about 20 near the polariton resonance (600 nm, 650 nm) and a factor of about 10 at the exciton wavelength (630 nm).

We now consider the IQE to determine the degree to which strong-coupling affects exciton transport and carrier extraction. Owing to the enhanced electric fields associated with polariton states, the electrode layers display parasitic absorption peaks (Supplementary Fig. 10). The IQE only reflects the charge collection process for photons absorbed in the WS2 active layer. IQE is calculated as the quotient of EQE and the percentage of photons absorbed in the separate WS2 layer under short-circuit conditions, and the percentage of photons dissipated in the separate WS2 layer can be extracted from layer-resolved absorption with the transfer matrix model (Supplementary Fig. 10). IQE decreases with increasing active layer thickness in conventional photovoltaic devices55–58. However, the IQE data in Fig. 3 show a strong oscillatory behavior with increasing WS2 thickness. For thin layers, both IQE and EQE exhibit lower values, partly due to (i) the limited light absorption of the thin material under weak coupling, (ii) more effects of interfacial defect recombination for thinner absorber layers, and (iii) contact-induced variability. Notably, A large increase in the IQE is observed as the thickness increases into the strong coupling regime, with a strong peak at the zero-detuning thickness for the first-order polariton. Near unity IQE is achieved for on-resonance devices. This enhancement arises from self-hybridized polariton states that concentrate optical fields within the WS2 layer, enabled by the device geometry used here.

We include in the IQE plots for Fig. 3 a phenomenological transport model (dashed line) to predict the effect of strong coupling enhanced transport as a function of WS2 thickness. Our model assumes a hopping-based exciton diffusion process in which a random walk occurs through a resonance energy transport (RET) mechanism14,59–61. Here, we expect that homogeneous RET occurs between identical but spatially separated molecules through the electric field associated with polariton states61. This concept is consistent with both the quantum electrodynamics formulation of RET and the concept of EPs62, in which the dipole-dipole interactions between light and matter can be interpreted as the rapid emission and reabsorption of cavity photons through excitons18. The resulting RET-based diffusivity is weighted by the thickness-dependent exciton fraction of the polariton branch and then multiplied by an exponentially decaying envelope function to represent free carriers having a greater chance of recombining in the bulk as thickness increases. This model is then fit to experimental data and represented as a phenomenological transport model in arbitrary units. We can use this model to qualitatively analyze the oscillatory trend of IQE-related diffusion coefficients at specific wavelengths and at which thicknesses the peaks are located. For more discussion of the transport model, please refer to the Supplementary Information (Supplementary Fig. 14). Figure 3b shows that the fitting results of the phenomenological model are in agreement with the trend of the experimental data, suggesting that the enhancement of the IQE is mainly due to improved exciton transport in the strong coupling regime.

Photovoltaic detection of polaritonic photodiodes
Finally, we evaluated the comprehensive detection performance of the exciton-polariton photodiode. Figure 4a shows the dark and optical current density curves for a representative device. The dark current density is as low as 5.33 × 10−7 A cm−2 at 0 V, indicating relatively low noise current and high sensitivity. Simultaneously, a light-switching ratio (Ion/Ioff ratio) of 7.1 × 105 is obtained. Compared with other exciton photodetectors, our photodiode exhibits lower dark current density and higher Ion/Ioff ratio (Supplementary Table 1). Fig. S15 (Supporting Information) presents the photocurrent versus light power for three representative devices operated in strong and weak coupling under 600 nm, 630 nm, and 650 nm illumination. The dependence of the photocurrent on the light intensity is fitted to a power law equation (y=bxα) from which α=1.01 to 1.04 is obtained. This confirms that the device has a good linear photovoltaic response, indicating high efficiency, as all the excited electrons/holes are captured by the electrodes before recombination63.

The responsivity (R) is closely related to strong coupling due to the benefits of increased absorption and polaritonic transport. Consequently, the trend observed in EQE should be mirrored in R. We calculated the variation of R with thickness for devices at wavelengths of 600 nm, 630 nm, and 650 nm when V=0 V is applied (Fig. 4b, Supplementary Fig. 16). This effect is confirmed by oscillatory behavior, with a significant increase in responsivity corresponding to polariton-induced transport. The maximum responsivity obtained is 0.35 A/W (600 nm, 15 μW), located near the first zero-detuned thicknesses. Additionally, there is a strong initial increase in responsivity as the strong coupling state is entered.

Noise equivalent power (NEP) is a key parameter for evaluating the ability of a photodetector to detect weak radiation and is defined as NEP=in/R (in is the dark current noise). Typically, dark current noise is caused by shot noise, thermal noise, and 1/f noise64. To fully account for frequency-dependent noise, the current noise power spectra of the device are measured at zero bias using a signal analyzer and a low-noise preamplifier (Supplementary Fig. 17). From the directly measured noise, we calculated in2 using the equation in2=B−1 ∫0B Sn(f)df where B is the bandwidth. Then we calculated the NEP at 0 V bias as shown in Fig. 4c. The NEP value is obtained to be 0.34 pW Hz−1/2 at WS2=73.5 nm under 630 nm illumination. The lower NEP indicates that the device has an excellent capability to distinguish between signal and noise, which can be achieved at high photoresponsivity and low current-noise power density.

Fast photoresponse is a key performance metric for photodetectors. We anticipate that the speed of the photodiode can be increased by utilizing enhanced transport through photonic modes. Therefore, we measured the response speed at a frequency of 10 kHz with a 520 nm laser at 0 V bias. As shown in Fig. 4d, we extracted the rise time as a function of WS2 thickness. The increase of the response speed in the strong-coupling state and the obvious peak at zero detuning thickness confirm the expected behavior. The fastest response in the strong coupling state is about 217 ns (WS2=73.5 nm). Supplementary Fig. 18 and Fig. 19 (Supporting Information) show numerous measurements of the response speed of a representative device in the strong- and weak-coupling states as well as typical response time curves, further confirming our conclusions. In addition, we obtained a −3dB cut-off frequency of 1.21 MHz (WS2=73.5 nm), which is extracted from the frequency-dependent photoresponse of the signal at a 520 nm laser at the modulation frequency as it drops to 70.7% of its initial value, as shown in Fig. 4e. The rise time τr can be estimated as 289.2 ns using the equation τr=0.35/f−3dB, which is similar to the response time measurement. Generally, the intrinsic lifetimes of excitons and polaritons fall within the picosecond-subnanosecond range, and the nanosecond-scale device photoresponse observed here was influenced by interfacial carrier trapping (Supplementary Fig. 20), suggesting that further suppression of interfacial defects can enable even faster operation. To further verify the performance enhancement of the polariton photodiode, we compared our device with other structures. Figure 4f shows the room temperature responsivity and response speed compared to other excitonic photodetectors. Our photodetectors both exhibit response times of several hundred nanoseconds at room temperature, which is faster than most excitonic photodetectors, as shown in Supplementary Table 3. Therefore, we can conclude that self-hybridized exciton polariton photodiodes are extremely attractive for high-efficiency, fast photodetection.
paper_content.methods:
Device fabrication
The bottom electrical contacts are patterned using electron-beam lithography and then electron-beam evaporation deposition of 3 nm Cr and 100 nm Au on a silicon substrate with 300 nm SiO2 (University Wafer). WS2 layers are mechanically exfoliated from bulk crystals (HQ Graphene) with blue adhesive film tape and transferred onto the surface of a polydimethylsiloxane stamp. WS2 layers are transferred by an all-dry deterministic transfer procedure onto the preprepared bottom electrical contacts by using a polydimethylsiloxane stamp. The top electrical contacts are patterned with electron beam lithography and ion beam sputtering deposition of 50 nm ITO. All devices after fabrication were annealed in an N2 environment. The resulting devices are identified by optical microscopy and later characterized by atomic force microscopy (AFM, Asylum Research MFP-3D Origin) to determine the flake thickness.

Reflectance measurements
The WS2 device reflectance spectra were measured using a home-built micro-reflection system (see Supplementary Fig. 21) with a 50× objective (Olympus, NA=0.45) under normal incidence. Dispersion relations in reflection were measured using a 100× objective (NA=0.9). The illumination source used in the measurements is 10–250 W tunable Quartz Tungsten Halogen lamps (Newport 66884 Research QTH Lamp), and the reflectance signals were gathered by a grating spectrometer equipped with a CCD (SpectraPro HRS-500). The reflectance spectra are normalized by the reflectance of a silver mirror (Thorlabs).

Determination of optical constants
The optical constants of ITO, Au used in our simulations are obtained by spectroscopic ellipsometry (Supplementary Fig. 2). The optical constants of WS2 are assumed to be thickness-independent bulk optical constants of WS2 from literature65. This is due to the fact that the phenomena reported in this study are concentrated in the 17–200 nm thickness range, which represents the electron bulk in WS2, as the effect of electron quantum confinement becomes negligible at about 5 nm (6–7 layers) thickness40.

Electrical and optoelectronic measurements
The light of a supercontinuum white light laser (Fianium White Lase SC400) is coupled into a tunable, high-resolution bandpass filter (LLTF Contrast SR-VIS-HP8). The resulting monochromatic beam was focused onto the WS2 device through a fixed optical path using a 20× objective lens (NA=0.45), producing a spot with a diameter of approximately 12 µm. Under short-circuit conditions, the photocurrent was amplified by a low-noise current preamplifier (Stanford Research Systems SR570) and subsequently analyzed using a lock-in amplifier (Stanford Research Systems SR865A) (shown in Supplementary Fig. 22). The EQE is determined by dividing the photocurrent of the WS2 device by the flux of incoming photons, which is obtained with calibrated silicon (Si) and indium–gallium–arsenide (InGaAs) photodiodes. For photocurrent mapping measurements, the laser beam was focused onto the device through a fixed optical path using a 50× objective lens (NA=0.6), yielding a laser spot diameter of approximately ~2 µm. The data on response time were acquired using a Tektronix MDO34 oscilloscope. The noise current spectrum was measured by using a preamplifier (DL1211) and a signal analyzer (Keysight N9010B) in a shielding box. The electronic characteristics were measured by a Keysight B2912A source. For low temperature measurements (up to 80 K), the samples were placed in a cryostat and cooled down to the desired temperature by controlling the flow of liquid nitrogen.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: The authors report self-hybridized exciton-polariton photodiodes based on multilayer WS2, in which transparent ITO electrodes act both as electrical contacts and anti-reflection coatings. Leveraging strong light-matter coupling, the devices exhibit broadband absorption and internal quantum efficiency (IQE) approaching unity near zero detuning. The EQE and IQE both show clear oscillatory behavior as a function of WS2 thickness, consistent with the dispersion of polaritonic modes. The photodiodes further demonstrate high responsivity, low noise-equivalent power, and fast response time (~217 ns), outperforming conventional excitonic photodetectors. These results suggest a promising design strategy for future exciton-based optoelectronics. The manuscript is technically sound and well-supported by experiments and simulations. However, the so-called “self-hybridized” concept has already appeared in many prior studies, which raises some concern about the novelty of this work. In addition, several specific issues require clarification or improvement before the manuscript can be considered for publication. 1. The IQE is derived from EQE and simulated absorption in WS2 using the transfer matrix method. The authors should more clearly state the assumptions behind isolating absorption in WS2, in particular whether parasitic absorption in ITO or Au has been considered or neglected. 2. In Figures 1b and S1, while the authors aim to demonstrate spatially uniform photocurrent response, the corresponding experimental conditions such as excitation wavelength, laser power, and beam spot size are missing. Even for qualitative measurements, all reported data should be scientifically valid and reproducible. 3. In Figure 2c, the x-axis is given in energy while all other spectra are plotted in wavelength. To ensure consistency and improve readability, the authors are strongly encouraged to present the data in wavelength units as well. 4. Although the reported response time of 217 ns is relatively fast among excitonic photodiodes, the term “ultrafast” is generally reserved for sub-nanosecond regimes. The authors should revise the manuscript to avoid overstatement of the device performance.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2: Zhao et al. report their findings on exciton–polariton photodiodes constructed from ITO/multilayer WS₂/Au structures and present measurements of several key optoelectronic parameters—including EQE, IQE, responsivity, and rise time—all of which exhibit peak values at a thickness corresponding to the emergence of possible polariton modes. The characterization of the devices is thorough, and the results demonstrate a high degree of internal consistency. However, attributing the observed phenomena to polaritons does not appear to be fully convincing, as some of the reported properties are not consistent with typical polariton behavior. In my view, the manuscript would benefit from further clarification and supporting evidence before it can be considered suitable for publication. 1. In Fig 2a and 2b, the authors present the simulated and measured polariton modes for different WS₂ thicknesses. They report an increase in the vacuum Rabi splitting with increasing WS₂ thickness. However, this trend raises several concerns. First, as the thickness of the WS₂ layer increases, the mode volume V of the cavity is expected to increase. Since the light–matter coupling strength g scales inversely with the square root of the mode volume (g∝1/\sqrt{V}), a larger mode volume should lead to a decrease in g, and thus a smaller Rabi splitting. Second, the exciton oscillator strength typically decreases in thicker flakes due to enhanced dielectric screening and a weakening of the direct K–K transition in WS₂. Therefore, one would also expect a reduction in g with increasing thickness. These considerations appear inconsistent with the observed trend and should be clarified by the authors. 2. Continuing from the previous point, the authors report a vacuum Rabi splitting of approximately 170 meV. However, even in optimized systems where monolayer WS₂ (or other TMDCs) is strongly coupled to a planar cavity, the vacuum Rabi splitting typically falls in the range of 40–60 meV (e.g. Nature Nano 17, 396-402 2022). In contrast, the authors observe a Rabi splitting that is nearly four times larger than these established values, despite using thicker WS₂ flakes, which generally exhibit reduced oscillator strength. This reported value appears unphysically large given the material system and cavity architecture, and the authors should provide further justification or supporting analysis to clarify this discrepancy. 3. In several figures (e.g., Fig. 2b, Fig. S5, Fig. S8), the authors use dashed lines as guides to the eye to indicate faint spectral features, presumably to suggest the presence of polariton modes. I recommend that the authors compute the first or second derivative of the signal with respect to energy (e.g., dI/dE or d2I/dE2), which is a widely used technique in the analysis of excitonic spectra. This approach could help reveal subtle features more clearly and provide stronger evidence for the existence of weak or overlapping polariton branches. 4. It would be helpful if the authors could provide the quality factor of their cavity. This parameter is essential for evaluating the cavity's optical performance and assessing whether the system operates in the strong coupling regime. Including this information would also facilitate comparison with previous studies. 5. In Fig. 2e, the authors present reflectance spectra at two different temperatures. Do the authors have data from a continuous temperature scan? Tracking the evolution of the polariton splitting as a function of temperature could provide additional evidence for the formation of polaritons. However, with only two temperature points shown, it is difficult to draw firm conclusions. A more comprehensive temperature-dependent analysis on a single device is encouraged. 6. In the optoelectronic measurements presented in Fig. 4, how do interfacial trap states between ITO and WS₂ affect the observed rise and response times? Given that exciton and polariton dynamics typically occur on picosecond to sub-nanosecond timescales, the reported response times on the order of hundreds of nanoseconds seem long (>> lifetime of exciton/polariton). This suggests that extrinsic effects, such as carrier trapping at the ITO/WS₂ interface, may play a significant role. The authors are encouraged to discuss the possible influence of interface quality and trap dynamics on the device performance.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3: The manuscript reports a polariton photodiode in a self-hybridized TMD system and clarifies that some device performances, particularly the response time (up to hundreds of nanoseconds), could be enhanced in the strong coupling regime. The experimental data primarily support the interpretation of cavity effect of enhancement rather than one based on polaritons. Although there are some decent performance improvements, the main merit appears to lie in the fast response time, which is significantly faster than reported devices. While the performance improvements are noted, the enhancement mechanism in the so called “strong coupling regime “ remains unclear, and the demonstrated evidence is not convincing. Below are my detailed comments: 1) The novelty of polariton photodiode bring out some concerns. In the context of exciton polariton photodiodes, this idea has been tried several years ago in organic excitonic materials [e.g., ACS Photonics 5, 2921-2927 (2018)]. Though it may be an interesting attempt to realize this idea within TMDs, the experimental evidence in this manuscript is not yet sufficient to support polariton effects. Further data and clarification are required to substantiate the role of polaritons in the observed performance enhancement. 2) Insufficient evidence for the strong coupling regime. To claim the strong coupling regime, the coupling strengths were fitted under different detuning by varying the TMD thicknesses. This is problematic. The strong coupling can be verified by satisfying the criterion that the coupling strengths should be larger than the averaged linewidths of cavity modes and excitons. This means the g^2 should be greater than (gamma_c^2+gamma_x^2)/2. This criterion has not been tested in their spectroscopic measurements (Figs. 2a-b). The criterion in the SI they cited can only infer there could be spectral splitting, which does not necessarily indicate the strong coupling regime (please see many references discussing about the differences between the intermediate coupling and the strong coupling). It is also important to note that the guidelines do not exactly follow the reflectivity dips (Fig. 2b), which are misleading. 3) The coupling strengths is proportional to the sample thickness, which has been varied by more than 8 times. For a rough estimation without considering the detailed cavity mode distributions (which was also ignored in the manuscript), the coupling strengths in Fig. 2b could be varied by about 3 times. In this way, the so-called anti-crossing features in Figs. 2a-b is misleading, as they do not share similar cavity strengths. It should be appropriate to measure samples of the same thickness at different angles (angle-resolved reflectivity) and then extract the coupling strength specifically for each thickness. 4) In Fig. 2d, the authors claim that the normalized EQE data support the consistency of polariton resonances and EQE peaks. However, this is not the case in close observations. For example, some EQE peaks coincide with the exciton resonance instead of so called “LP” or “UP” states. To substantiate the polariton effect, it is strongly suggested that they should first clarify the well-separated polariton peaks by checking the criterion of the strong coupling regime, which are expected to be distant from the exciton resonances with respect to their linewidths. For instance, some convincing measurements should be at least performed in the “zero-detuning” samples to better determine the strong coupling regime. 5) In Fig. 2f, some error bars are excessively large, which are greater than the data variations. This largely undermines the reliability of the data and makes it difficult to draw convincing conclusions. The authors are strongly recommended to retake the data, and thus effectively reduce these error margins and provide more precise data to support their claims. 6) To strengthen the argument for a polariton-based photodiode, the correlation between the enhanced performances and the polariton states should be unambiguously established. In Figs 3, 4b, and 4d, the performance improvement in the device seems more likely to be due to cavity resonance rather than polariton formation. At the zero-detuning, the peak device performance coincides with the exact cavity resonance (in Fig. S9), indicating that cavity enhancement might be the optimized. This does not necessarily lead to polariton effects. To establish the polariton enhancements, demonstrating the optimized formation of polaritons and unambiguously identifying the peaks of performance parameters at the polariton states would be critical. 7) The comparisons with reported device performance seem to be suspicious. In their comparisons, the on/off ratio, dark current density, especially response time seems to be much larger than reported TMD-based photodiodes/photodetectors. However, there are some mistakes in SI that comparisons of device parameters with previously reported devices show several discrepancies. For instance, in SI Reference 20 [Adv. Electron. Mater. 7, 2000964 (2021)], the responsivity is given as 777 mA/W. But the manuscript lists it as 360 mA/W (SI Table S2). As another example, the responsivity in SI Reference 8 [Appl. Surf. Sci. 481, 1127-1132 (2019)] is reported to be about 5 orders of magnitude higher than this work. But the manuscript totally ignored it in the comparisons of responsivity (SI Table S2). The similar inconsistencies must be addressed and ensure all comparative data are correct and well-cited without such suspicious discrepancies. I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. Response to Reviewer 1
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors report self-hybridized exciton-polariton photodiodes based on multilayer
WS , in which transparent ITO electrodes act both as electrical contacts and anti-
2
reflection coatings. Leveraging strong light-matter coupling, the devices exhibit
broadband absorption and internal quantum efficiency (IQE) approaching unity near
zero detuning. The EQE and IQE both show clear oscillatory behavior as a function of
WS thickness, consistent with the dispersion of polaritonic modes. The photodiodes
2
further demonstrate high responsivity, low noise-equivalent power, and fast response
time (~217 ns), outperforming conventional excitonic photodetectors. These results
suggest a promising design strategy for future exciton-based optoelectronics. The
manuscript is technically sound and well-supported by experiments and simulations.
However, the so-called “self-hybridized” concept has already appeared in many prior
studies, which raises some concern about the novelty of this work. In addition, several
specific issues require clarification or improvement before the manuscript can be
considered for publication.
Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the constructive feedback and for recognizing the
technical strength, experimental rigor, and simulation support of our manuscript. We
appreciate the positive evaluation of our device performance, including the high
responsivity, low noise-equivalent power, and fast response time, as well as the
reviewer’s recognition of the potential impact of our results on future exciton-based
optoelectronic design strategies.
About the innovations:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for pointing out this issue regarding novelty. While
we agree that the concept of self-hybridized exciton-polaritons has been reported in
prior optical studies (Refs. [34,35,40,41] in our manuscript), we would like to
emphasize that our work represents the first demonstration of a self-hybridized
exciton-polariton effect for photovoltaic detection with high responsivity, low
noise-equivalent power, and fast response time. The key advances of our study can
be summarized as follows, and to further highlight these advantages, we compared our
devices with a recently reported work published in Nature Materials (Intrinsic strong
light-matter coupling with self-hybridized bound states in the continuum in van der
Waals metasurfaces)：
Figure R1.1. A comparison between the strategies in the previous reported work
(Nat. Mater. 22, 970–976 (2023)) and our work.
a) Device-level realization with an open-cavity architecture:
Previous reports mainly focused on spectroscopic observation of self-
hybridized polaritons in TMDC multilayers or perovskites, typically limited to
reflectance or absorption measurements. In contrast, our work integrates this
phenomenon into a functional photodiode architecture, directly correlating
the polaritonic dispersion with EQE and IQE performance metrics, which
have not been shown before. This closes the critical gap between spectroscopic
phenomena and practical exciton-polariton-based optoelectronics, offering a
compact and fabrication-friendly architecture.
b) Concurrent broadband absorption and transport enhancement:
We show that the ITO electrode simultaneously acts as a transparent contact
and anti-reflection coating, enabling broadband absorption beyond the narrow
exciton resonance. More importantly, the polariton states are exploited to
overcome the intrinsic exciton diffusion bottleneck, leading to near-unity
IQE and a dramatic enhancement in responsivity. This functionality is enabled
solely by the intrinsic optical properties of WS and the tailored ITO electrode
2
integration, without additional photonic structures such as DBRs or plasmonic
metal cavities.
c) Near-unity internal quantum efficiency via tuning of coupling conditions

condition (Fig. R1.2). These results show parasitic absorption in both ITO and Au at
the upper polariton (UP) and the lower polariton (LP) resonances, with losses at the LP
resonance where the WS extinction coefficient decreases below the exciton energy.

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
Zhao et al. report their findings on exciton–polariton photodiodes constructed from
ITO/multilayer WS /Au structures and present measurements of several key
2
optoelectronic parameters—including EQE, IQE, responsivity, and rise time—all of
which exhibit peak values at a thickness corresponding to the emergence of possible
polariton modes. The characterization of the devices is thorough, and the results
demonstrate a high degree of internal consistency. However, attributing the observed
phenomena to polaritons does not appear to be fully convincing, as some of the reported
properties are not consistent with typical polariton behavior. In my view, the manuscript
would benefit from further clarification and supporting evidence before it can be
considered suitable for publication.
Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for their thoughtful and thorough evaluation of our
manuscript. We greatly appreciate the positive comments on the quality of device
fabrication, the comprehensive characterization, and the internal consistency of the
results. Your critical feedback, particularly regarding the attribution of our results to
exciton-polariton modes, has been extremely valuable in helping us refine our
interpretations and improve the clarity and rigor of the manuscript.
In response, we have carefully addressed each of your concerns and revised the
manuscript accordingly. Below, we provide detailed responses to each specific point,
including additional clarifications and supporting evidence. We hope that the revised
version meets your expectations and more clearly conveys the significance of our
findings.
1. In Fig 2a and 2b, the authors present the simulated and measured polariton modes
for different WS thicknesses. They report an increase in the vacuum Rabi splitting with
2
increasing WS thickness. However, this trend raises several concerns. First, as the
2
thickness of the WS layer increases, the mode volume V of the cavity is expected to
2
increase. Since the light-matter coupling strength 𝑔 scales inversely with the square
root of the mode volume (𝑔 ∝ 1/√𝑉), a larger mode volume should lead to a decrease
in 𝑔, and thus a smaller Rabi splitting. Second, the exciton oscillator strength typically
decreases in thicker flakes due to enhanced dielectric screening and a weakening of the
direct K-K transition in WS . Therefore, one would also expect a reduction in 𝑔 with
2
increasing thickness. These considerations appear inconsistent with the observed trend
and should be clarified by the authors.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for raising this important and insightful question. While the
intuitive picture is that a larger mode volume weakens the coupling strength, in our case
multiple cooperative effects, such as the increased number of excitons participating in
the interaction and the improved overlap with the optical field, work together to
reinforce the coupling, leading to the observed enhancement in vacuum Rabi splitting.
Specifically:
(1) Cooperative scaling of mode volume (V ) and exciton number (N):
Indeed, it is correct in principle that, for a fixed number of excitons N, an increase in
the mode volume V leads to a reduction in the light-matter coupling strength, as
described by the relation:

2. Continuing from the previous point, the authors report a vacuum Rabi splitting of
approximately 170 meV. However, even in optimized systems where monolayer WS
2
(or other TMDCs) is strongly coupled to a planar cavity, the vacuum Rabi splitting
typically falls in the range of 40-60 meV (e.g. Nature Nano 17, 396-402 2022). In
contrast, the authors observe a Rabi splitting that is nearly four times larger than these
established values, despite using thicker WS flakes, which generally exhibit reduced
2
oscillator strength. This reported value appears unphysically large given the material
system and cavity architecture, and the authors should provide further justification or
supporting analysis to clarify this discrepancy.
Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for this important and insightful point. We confirm that
the large vacuum Rabi splitting of ~170 meV observed in our system is physically
reasonable and consistent with both theory and recent literature. Although this value
exceeds the typical 40-60 meV reported for monolayer TMDC-cavity systems, it is
attributed to enhanced collective coupling of exciton in our multilayer self-
hybridized geometry. Specifically:
1) Key differences from monolayer-cavity systems:
We agree that monolayer WS exhibits a higher per-exciton oscillator strength
2
compared to bulk flakes. However, the total light-matter coupling strength 𝑔, and
consequently the vacuum Rabi splitting, is determined not only by the oscillator
strength per exciton but also by the total number of participating excitons 𝑁, and
the optical mode volume 𝑉. This relationship is well established in the literature
(e.g., Refs. [Nat. Mater. 22, 970–976 (2023); Phys. Rev. B 107, 075415; Nat.
Commun. 13, 5597 (2022)]) following the relation:
𝑁
𝑔 ∝ √
𝑉
In monolayer-based systems, despite the strong oscillator strength of a single
exciton, the number of available emitters N is extremely limited due to the atomic
thickness of the film. In contrast, in our system, the cavity is self-hybridized and
composed of multilayer WS , with thicknesses >50 nm, placing the system well into
2
the quasi-bulk regime. While the per-exciton oscillator strength may be lower, the
number of participating excitons is significantly greater.
In this structure, the exciton number 𝑁 is significantly higher than that of the
monolayer-based system. Meanwhile, the cavity mode volume 𝑉 does not increase
significantly compared with the conventional Fabry-Pérot cavity. Therefore, the
overall coupling strength is significantly enhanced. This structure leads us to
observe a vacuum Rabi splitting of approximately 170 meV, which is a
manifestation of enhanced exciton collective coupling in thick-layer TMDC
systems (see Table R2.2).
2) Literature precedent for large Rabi splitting in thick TMDC systems:
Our observation of a ~170 meV vacuum Rabi splitting is consistent with recent
studies on self-hybridized polaritonic systems involving thick TMDC films.
Notably, Munkhbat et al. (ACS Photonics 6, 139-147, 2019) and others (Phys. Rev.
B 107, 075415, 2023; Nat. Commun. 13, 5597, 2022) have reported that strong
collective coupling in such systems can lead to significantly enhanced Rabi splitting,
often exceeding those of monolayer-based systems.
These findings confirm that large Rabi splitting in the >100 meV range is
physically reasonable and achievable in TMDC systems with similar architectures.
3) Extraction of Rabi splitting:
To ensure the reliability of the extracted Rabi splitting, we performed new angle-
resolved reflectivity spectra and fitted the polariton dispersion using a standard
coupled oscillator model. Both the upper and lower polariton branches were well
reproduced by the model (see Fig. R2.3). The extracted Rabi splitting is 151.4 meV,
178.8 meV, and 186.1 meV, respectively (see Table R2.2).
This consistency between experimental observation and theoretical modeling
further supports the physical validity of the large Rabi splitting reported in our work.

4. It would be helpful if the authors could provide the quality factor of their cavity. This
parameter is essential for evaluating the cavity's optical performance and assessing
whether the system operates in the strong coupling regime. Including this information
would also facilitate comparison with previous studies.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. The cavity quality factors were
extracted from the linewidths of the cavity modes in the wavelength domain.
Specifically, the full width at half maximum (FWHM) of each cavity resonance, Δλ,
was obtained and converted into the quality factor using Q=λ /Δλ, where λ is the
0 0
resonance wavelength. We calculate this from TMM at a λ of 800 nm (off resonance)
0
for each cavity mode. This procedure yields approximate Q values of 16, 20, and 25 for
the first-, second-, and third-order modes, respectively.
These quality factors are reasonable for self-hybridized cavity systems and are
sufficient to support the formation of polariton states. This conclusion is further
supported by the linewidths analyzed in the energy domain, where the measured
vacuum Rabi splitting significantly exceeds the combined cavity and exciton linewidths,
thereby fulfilling the strong coupling criterion. For self-hybridized cavities, future work
will need to focus on strategies such as optimizing material interface quality, employing
lower-loss active materials, or engineering photonic structures with better in-plane
confinement to further enhance the quality factor.
Revised:
We have now included the above information regarding the cavity Q factors in the
revised manuscript (see Supplementary Information, Page 5).

We thank the reviewer for raising this important point regarding the difference between
the intrinsic exciton/polariton dynamics and the device-level response time observed in
Fig. 4. To clarify this issue, we conducted a series of additional experiments to evaluate
the influence of interfacial trap states and extrinsic defects on both exciton lifetime and
photoresponse dynamics.
Indeed, while exciton and polariton lifetimes typically lie in the picosecond–sub-
nanosecond regime, the observed rise and response time in Fig. 4 are longer (hundreds
of nanoseconds), indicating the presence of extrinsic limiting mechanisms. The rise and
fall times in photodetectors are generally governed not only by the intrinsic
exciton/polariton dynamics but also by carrier trapping and detrapping at
interfaces and surfaces, as well as carrier transport within the device channel.
These defect states are inevitably introduced during device fabrication.
To investigate the influence of interfacial defect states on the lifetime of
exciton/polariton and response time of exciton-polariton devices, we prepared two
devices from the same nanosheet (Fig. R2.8d): pristine WS nanosheets obtained by
2
mechanical exfoliation, and the same WS nanosheets subjected to 23 s of oxygen
2
plasma treatment, emulating the defect formation typically induced during ITO
sputtering. The surface morphology was examined using atomic force microscopy
(AFM) (Fig. R2.8). The WS thickness was measured to be 79.9 nm (Fig. R2.8a). Root-
2
mean-square (r.m.s.) roughness analysis revealed that the pristine WS nanosheet
2
exhibited an atomically clean surface with an r.m.s. roughness of 0.31 nm (Fig. R2.8
fb). After O plasma treatment, the r.m.s. roughness increased to 1.02 nm (Fig. R2.8
2
fc), indicating surface degradation and the formation of uniformly distributed defects.
The rise and response times of a photodetector are fundamentally governed by
intrinsic material dynamics. Although the lifetimes of excitons and polaritons typically
lie in the picosecond-to-sub-nanosecond range, interfacial carrier trapping at the
ITO/WS interface and the subsequent slow release of trapped carriers can prolong
2
the overall photocurrent response. In our case, plasma treatment increases the density
of interfacial trap states, which accelerates recombination (shortening the
exciton/polariton lifetime (Fig. R2.8e)) while simultaneously slowing net carrier
extraction and transport due to transient trapping-detrapping dynamics. These trap
states delay carrier collection and extend the photocurrent response into the
nanosecond regime, consistent with the features observed in Fig. R2.8 f. Nevertheless,
the response times of our devices remain much faster than those of most other excitonic
photodetectors (main text, Fig.4f).
Although the response speed is still below the theoretical limit owing to the group
velocity of polaritons, our additional data strengthen the validity of the results and
highlight the promise of this approach for future studies. Future research should focus
on reducing carrier trapping at the ITO/WS interface and optimizing the relaxation
2
dynamics of exciton/polaritonic states, such as suppressing non-radiative losses,
extending lifetimes, and promoting rapid energy transfer, to further enhance the
generation and transport efficiency of photogenerated carriers. Potential strategies to
mitigate interfacial defects include adopting physical transfer of electrodes to avoid
plasma-induced damage, introducing ultrathin interfacial passivation layers,
employing van der Waals contacts, or using chemical surface treatments to reduce
trap density. Such improvements are expected to markedly shorten the rise time of the
photoresponse, which is particularly critical for the development of sub-nanosecond,
fast photodiodes for applications in optical communication and sensing. These
improvements are expected to fully unlock the potential of polariton-enhanced
transport in next-generation optoelectronic devices and shorten the rise time of the
photoresponse, which is particularly critical for the development of sub-nanosecond,
fast photodiodes for optical communication and sensing applications.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
The manuscript reports a polariton photodiode in a self-hybridized TMD system and
clarifies that some device performances, particularly the response time (up to hundreds
of nanoseconds), could be enhanced in the strong coupling regime. The experimental
data primarily support the interpretation of cavity effect of enhancement rather than one
based on polaritons. Although there are some decent performance improvements, the
main merit appears to lie in the fast response time, which is significantly faster than
reported devices. While the performance improvements are noted, the enhancement
mechanism in the so called “strong coupling regime” remains unclear, and the
demonstrated evidence is not convincing. Below are my detailed comments:
Response:
We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful and critical evaluation of our manuscript. We
sincerely appreciate the recognition of the fast response time and performance
improvements in our polariton photodiodes. We understand the reviewer’s concern
regarding the attribution of device enhancements to strong light-matter coupling rather
than purely to cavity effects. In the revised manuscript, we have taken substantial steps
to clarify the physical mechanisms underlying the observed enhancements and to
further distinguish the role of polaritonic modes from conventional cavity-induced
effects. We would also like to point out that while evidence of polaritons in the
optoelectronic responses in these devices is clear, the true merit in terms of performance
(response speed) is still far from theoretical values due to imperfect materials and
interfaces. Optimization of materials and related interfaces is beyond the scope of
current work and will be part of future efforts.
We have expanded our analysis to include:
a) Temperature-dependent reflectance spectra (87-300 K), which
demonstrate continuous, non-collapsing mode splitting consistent with
polariton branches rather than Fabry-Pérot resonances (see revised Fig. 2e and
Supplementary Fig. S13).
b) Angle-resolved dispersion mapping and coupled oscillator model
fitting, producing Rabi splitting values that are reproducible and consistent
across several independent experimental methods, further confirming the
presence of strong coupling (see revised Supplementary Fig. S6).
c) The relationship between reflectance spectra and EQE demonstrates
photoresponse and quantum efficiency enhancements that correlate well with
the dispersion of polariton modes (see revised Fig. 2c).
These revisions are described in detail in our responses to the specific comments
below, and the corresponding modifications have been incorporated throughout the
manuscript. We hope these additions provide a clearer picture of how the strong
coupling between excitons and photons contributes to the observed optoelectronic
performance enhancements.
1) The novelty of polariton photodiode bring out some concerns. In the context of
exciton polariton photodiodes, this idea has been tried several years ago in organic
excitonic materials [e.g., ACS Photonics 5, 2921-2927 (2018)]. Though it may be an
interesting attempt to realize this idea within TMDs, the experimental evidence in this
manuscript is not yet sufficient to support polariton effects. Further data and
clarification are required to substantiate the role of polaritons in the observed
performance enhancement.
Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for acknowledging our effort to explore polariton
photodiodes within the TMD material system. We appreciate the reference to prior work
on organic excitonic materials, such as ACS Photonics 5, 2921-2927 (2018), which
indeed laid important groundwork in this area.
While the concept of exciton-polariton photodetectors has been previously
demonstrated in organic systems, our work presents a fundamentally distinct strategy.
It is also worth noting that organic excitonic semiconductors cannot achieve self-
hybridization due to low values of real part of refractive indices and therefore always
have to rely on closed Fabry-Perot cavity systems. Further the
nanocrystalline/amorphous nature of organic semiconductors obfuscates the transport
of excitons. In contrast WS has high real part of refractive index and exciton transport
2
is highly anisotropic in v.s. out of plane making it a much better model system for
investigating polariton and strong coupling effects in photodiode and photovoltaic
devices.
As shown in Figure R3.1, unlike metal-mirror organic polariton photodiodes that rely
on a closed Fabry-Pérot cavity (ACS Photonics 5, 2921-2927 (2018)) and whose
internal quantum efficiency is limited by Ag electrode losses, our device realizes
cavity-free self-hybridized (our work) polaritons in multilayer WS , where a single
architecture not only yields dispersive, thickness-quantized polaritons whose extrema
align with EQE/IQE oscillations and near-unity IQE at zero detuning but also delivers
device-level advantages, high responsivity (~ 0.35 A/W), low NEP (~0.34 pW Hz-
1/2), and sub-μs response (~217 ns), which were not accessible in previous
demonstrations (ACS Photonics 5, 2921-2927 (2018)).

splitting that persists with temperature, which is inconsistent with Fabry-Pérot
resonances but fully consistent with polariton branches.

Finally, we explicitly correlate the polariton dispersion with device-level
metrics by showing that the enhancements in EQE spectra occur at energies that
coincide with the polariton branches (Fig. 2c-d; see also Fig. R3.5). Figure
R3.5a shows the coupled oscillator model fit, along with the experimental EQE
peak wavelengths extracted from a range of device thicknesses. Notably, the
peak response positions of the EQE spectra in devices with varying thicknesses
(scattered dots) exhibit excellent agreement with the theoretical model (dashed
lines). In particular, the evolution of their wavelength positions with thickness
strictly follows the characteristic dispersion relation of polaritons, with the peak
positions corresponding to the resonance modes of the UP and LP branches,
respectively. This consistency between experimental observations and the
theoretical model provides solid evidence that the polariton state enhances light-
trapping efficiency by modulating photon-exciton interactions, clearly
demonstrating the crucial role of polariton engineering in improving photodiode
performance. Figure R3.5b shows the EQE spectra of three representative
devices, one in the weak coupling regime, one near zero detuning for the first
order polariton, and one near zero detuning for the second order polariton. In
these strongly coupled devices, both the lower polariton branch (LPB) and
upper polariton branch (UPB) exhibit spectral separations from the bare exciton
resonance that exceed their respective linewidths. This clear spectral separation
enables unambiguous identification of the polariton branches. The responses
below the bare exciton energy of the strongly coupled devices can be observed,
and the peaks of the responses correspond to the reflectance minima (attributed
to UP and LP branches) reported in the Fig.R3.5c. These features are absent in
weakly coupled devices, confirming that all these responses are dominated by
the E-P states. This direct correspondence between optical dispersion and
photoresponse provides strong evidence that the observed performance
enhancements stem from polariton-assisted absorption and transport, rather
than from conventional cavity effects.

6) To strengthen the argument for a polariton-based photodiode, the correlation
between the enhanced performances and the polariton states should be unambiguously
established. In Figs 3, 4b, and 4d, the performance improvement in the device seems
more likely to be due to cavity resonance rather than polariton formation. At the zero-
detuning, the peak device performance coincides with the exact cavity resonance (in
Fig. S9), indicating that cavity enhancement might be the optimized. This does not
necessarily lead to polariton effects. To establish the polariton enhancements,
demonstrating the optimized formation of polaritons and unambiguously identifying
the peaks of performance parameters at the polariton states would be critical.
Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the insightful comment regarding the need to
unambiguously establish the correlation between enhanced device performance and
polariton states. We fully agree that distinguishing between cavity resonance effects and
polariton formation is critical to strengthen the argument for a polariton photodiode.
While cavity resonances can indeed enhance the local optical field, our data
demonstrate that strong exciton-photon coupling leads to polariton states whose
influence extends beyond what is expected from bare cavity effects alone. Finally, we
would also like to point out that while evidence of polaritons in the optoelectronic
responses in these devices is clear, the true merit in terms of performance (response
speed) is still far from theoretical values due to imperfect materials and interfaces.
Optimization of materials and related interfaces is beyond the scope of current work
and will be part of future efforts.
Below we address the reviewer’s concerns with additional evidence supporting the
polaritonic origin of the enhancements.
1) Zero-detuning devices provide unambiguous evidence.
In the absence of strong coupling, cavity resonance enhances only a single optical
mode without splitting, leading merely to a strengthened resonance peak (Fig.
R3.13 c,d; device of 39.6 nm). By contrast, exciton-polariton formation results
in the emergence of distinct lower and upper polariton branches (LP/UP)
separated by a Rabi splitting (Fig. R3.13 c,d; device of 77.9 nm and 151.2 nm).
In representative zero-detuning devices (e.g. WS thicknesses of 77.9 nm and
2
151.2 nm, corresponding approximately to the first- and second-order maxima ),
the LP/UP are well resolved (see Fig.R3.13a,b) and the reflectance minima
(polariton modes, see Fig.R3.13c) show a one-to-one correspondence with EQE
maxima (see Fig.R3.4 d) , confirming that the photoresponse in these devices is
dominated by exciton-polariton states. The extracted couplings (≈92 and 93.5
meV) satisfy the strong coupling criteria. Owing to exciton-polariton formation,
strongly coupled devices can harvest more photons in the spectral region near the
bandgap. Compared with conventional cavity resonance, this approach avoids the
narrowband absorption inherent to cavity enhancement and the limitation of high
absorption efficiency only at specific wavelengths. As a result, both the cut-off
wavelength is extended, and near-unity internal quantum efficiency is achieved
for on-resonance devices (see Fig.R3.13d). The observed performance
enhancement in these devices cannot be explained by a single uncoupled cavity
mode.

4) Persistence of strong coupling across temperature.
To capture the full thermal evolution of these coupled states, we carried out
continuous temperature-dependent reflectance spectroscopy from 87 K to 300 K
on WS cavities with thicknesses ranging from ∼35 nm to ∼130 nm (see Fig.
display smooth, monotonic redshift with increasing temperature. Importantly, the
polariton branches remain spectrally resolved over the entire temperature range
without collapsing into a single peak, confirming that the system persistently
resides in the strong-coupling regime. The temperature-induced evolution of the
spectral splitting is accompanied by consistent trends in the EQE spectra
(Fig.R3.16 c, Fig.R3.17) with devices near zero detuning exhibiting distinct peak
splitting even at elevated temperatures. In both strong- and weak-coupling
devices, the EQE spectra exhibits a pronounced steepening of the exciton
absorption edges, a blue shift of the absorption maxima, and an enhancement of
the EQE at low temperatures under both resonant and non-resonant excitation,
reflecting strengthened excitonic and polaritonic effects. Correspondingly, the
absorption peaks dominated by the upper and lower polariton branches (UP and
LP) are also clearly resolved in the EQE spectra, as indicated by the black arrows
in Fig. R3.16c and Fig. R3.17. These observations substantiate the assignment of
the observed features to robust exciton-photon hybrid states (polaritons), rather
than to uncoupled optical modes or interference fringes. The observed
temperature dependence is consistent across multiple devices with different WS
2
thicknesses, demonstrating the robustness of the polaritonic features and the
generality of the self-hybridized cavity design.

8 [Appl. Surf. Sci. 481, 1127-1132 (2019)] is reported to be about 5 orders of magnitude

Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the careful reading and pointing out the
inconsistencies in the supplementary comparisons. We have carefully reviewed and
cross-checked all cited references and comparative data in SI Table S2. The following
modifications have been made:
a) Correction of Ref. 20 [Adv. Electron. Mater. 7, 2000964 (2021)]:
The responsivity value for this reference was mistakenly listed as 360 mA/W in
SI Table S2 (corrected in the revised SI Table S3). We sincerely apologize for this
mistake. Notably, in the previous version of the manuscript, the correct value of
777 mA/W was already cited in Fig. 4f of the main text (shown as the cyan circle
in the lower right corner). We have now corrected the supplementary table to
ensure full consistency.
b) Discussion of Ref. 8 [Appl. Surf. Sci. 481, 1127-1132 (2019)]:
The high responsivity reported in this work (>1000 A/W) arises mainly from
Au-based localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) enhancement combined
with photoconductive gain under high external bias, rather than from intrinsic
excitonic processes of the active material. Since our devices, and those included in
SI Table S2 (corrected in the revised SI Table S3), focus on exciton-driven
photocurrent mechanisms, direct comparison with plasmonic-enhanced
responsivity values and photoconductive gain under high external bias would not
provide a fair or physically meaningful benchmark of intrinsic device performance.
Therefore, to maintain a consistent and relevant comparison framework, this
reference has been excluded from the revised supplementary tables (SI Table S2
and S3), with the rationale explicitly noted.
c) Verification of all other references:
We have carefully re-checked all remaining references and ensured that each
parameter is now accurately quoted and consistently cited without discrepancy.
These revisions are now clearly marked in the updated supplementary
information (Table S3). We apologize for the oversight and have taken extra care
to ensure that all comparisons are now consistent, fair, and transparent. These
corrections do not affect the main conclusions of our work but reinforce the rigor
and reliability of our analysis.
