## Methods

Device fabrication
The bottom electrical contacts are patterned using electron-beam lithography and then electron-beam evaporation deposition of 3 nm Cr and 100 nm Au on a silicon substrate with 300 nm SiO2 (University Wafer). WS2 layers are mechanically exfoliated from bulk crystals (HQ Graphene) with blue adhesive film tape and transferred onto the surface of a polydimethylsiloxane stamp. WS2 layers are transferred by an all-dry deterministic transfer procedure onto the preprepared bottom electrical contacts by using a polydimethylsiloxane stamp. The top electrical contacts are patterned with electron beam lithography and ion beam sputtering deposition of 50 nm ITO. All devices after fabrication were annealed in an N2 environment. The resulting devices are identified by optical microscopy and later characterized by atomic force microscopy (AFM, Asylum Research MFP-3D Origin) to determine the flake thickness.

Reflectance measurements
The WS2 device reflectance spectra were measured using a home-built micro-reflection system (see Supplementary Fig. 21) with a 50× objective (Olympus, NA=0.45) under normal incidence. Dispersion relations in reflection were measured using a 100× objective (NA=0.9). The illumination source used in the measurements is 10–250 W tunable Quartz Tungsten Halogen lamps (Newport 66884 Research QTH Lamp), and the reflectance signals were gathered by a grating spectrometer equipped with a CCD (SpectraPro HRS-500). The reflectance spectra are normalized by the reflectance of a silver mirror (Thorlabs).

Determination of optical constants
The optical constants of ITO, Au used in our simulations are obtained by spectroscopic ellipsometry (Supplementary Fig. 2). The optical constants of WS2 are assumed to be thickness-independent bulk optical constants of WS2 from literature65. This is due to the fact that the phenomena reported in this study are concentrated in the 17–200 nm thickness range, which represents the electron bulk in WS2, as the effect of electron quantum confinement becomes negligible at about 5 nm (6–7 layers) thickness40.

Electrical and optoelectronic measurements
The light of a supercontinuum white light laser (Fianium White Lase SC400) is coupled into a tunable, high-resolution bandpass filter (LLTF Contrast SR-VIS-HP8). The resulting monochromatic beam was focused onto the WS2 device through a fixed optical path using a 20× objective lens (NA=0.45), producing a spot with a diameter of approximately 12 µm. Under short-circuit conditions, the photocurrent was amplified by a low-noise current preamplifier (Stanford Research Systems SR570) and subsequently analyzed using a lock-in amplifier (Stanford Research Systems SR865A) (shown in Supplementary Fig. 22). The EQE is determined by dividing the photocurrent of the WS2 device by the flux of incoming photons, which is obtained with calibrated silicon (Si) and indium–gallium–arsenide (InGaAs) photodiodes. For photocurrent mapping measurements, the laser beam was focused onto the device through a fixed optical path using a 50× objective lens (NA=0.6), yielding a laser spot diameter of approximately ~2 µm. The data on response time were acquired using a Tektronix MDO34 oscilloscope. The noise current spectrum was measured by using a preamplifier (DL1211) and a signal analyzer (Keysight N9010B) in a shielding box. The electronic characteristics were measured by a Keysight B2912A source. For low temperature measurements (up to 80 K), the samples were placed in a cryostat and cooled down to the desired temperature by controlling the flow of liquid nitrogen.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

The authors report self-hybridized exciton-polariton photodiodes based on multilayer WS2, in which transparent ITO electrodes act both as electrical contacts and anti-reflection coatings. Leveraging strong light-matter coupling, the devices exhibit broadband absorption and internal quantum efficiency (IQE) approaching unity near zero detuning. The EQE and IQE both show clear oscillatory behavior as a function of WS2 thickness, consistent with the dispersion of polaritonic modes. The photodiodes further demonstrate high responsivity, low noise-equivalent power, and fast response time (~217 ns), outperforming conventional excitonic photodetectors. These results suggest a promising design strategy for future exciton-based optoelectronics. The manuscript is technically sound and well-supported by experiments and simulations. However, the so-called “self-hybridized” concept has already appeared in many prior studies, which raises some concern about the novelty of this work. In addition, several specific issues require clarification or improvement before the manuscript can be considered for publication. 1. The IQE is derived from EQE and simulated absorption in WS2 using the transfer matrix method. The authors should more clearly state the assumptions behind isolating absorption in WS2, in particular whether parasitic absorption in ITO or Au has been considered or neglected. 2. In Figures 1b and S1, while the authors aim to demonstrate spatially uniform photocurrent response, the corresponding experimental conditions such as excitation wavelength, laser power, and beam spot size are missing. Even for qualitative measurements, all reported data should be scientifically valid and reproducible. 3. In Figure 2c, the x-axis is given in energy while all other spectra are plotted in wavelength. To ensure consistency and improve readability, the authors are strongly encouraged to present the data in wavelength units as well. 4. Although the reported response time of 217 ns is relatively fast among excitonic photodiodes, the term “ultrafast” is generally reserved for sub-nanosecond regimes. The authors should revise the manuscript to avoid overstatement of the device performance.

### Reviewer 2

Zhao et al. report their findings on exciton–polariton photodiodes constructed from ITO/multilayer WS₂/Au structures and present measurements of several key optoelectronic parameters—including EQE, IQE, responsivity, and rise time—all of which exhibit peak values at a thickness corresponding to the emergence of possible polariton modes. The characterization of the devices is thorough, and the results demonstrate a high degree of internal consistency. However, attributing the observed phenomena to polaritons does not appear to be fully convincing, as some of the reported properties are not consistent with typical polariton behavior. In my view, the manuscript would benefit from further clarification and supporting evidence before it can be considered suitable for publication. 1. In Fig 2a and 2b, the authors present the simulated and measured polariton modes for different WS₂ thicknesses. They report an increase in the vacuum Rabi splitting with increasing WS₂ thickness. However, this trend raises several concerns. First, as the thickness of the WS₂ layer increases, the mode volume V of the cavity is expected to increase. Since the light–matter coupling strength g scales inversely with the square root of the mode volume (g∝1/\sqrt{V}), a larger mode volume should lead to a decrease in g, and thus a smaller Rabi splitting. Second, the exciton oscillator strength typically decreases in thicker flakes due to enhanced dielectric screening and a weakening of the direct K–K transition in WS₂. Therefore, one would also expect a reduction in g with increasing thickness. These considerations appear inconsistent with the observed trend and should be clarified by the authors. 2. Continuing from the previous point, the authors report a vacuum Rabi splitting of approximately 170 meV. However, even in optimized systems where monolayer WS₂ (or other TMDCs) is strongly coupled to a planar cavity, the vacuum Rabi splitting typically falls in the range of 40–60 meV (e.g. Nature Nano 17, 396-402 2022). In contrast, the authors observe a Rabi splitting that is nearly four times larger than these established values, despite using thicker WS₂ flakes, which generally exhibit reduced oscillator strength. This reported value appears unphysically large given the material system and cavity architecture, and the authors should provide further justification or supporting analysis to clarify this discrepancy. 3. In several figures (e.g., Fig. 2b, Fig. S5, Fig. S8), the authors use dashed lines as guides to the eye to indicate faint spectral features, presumably to suggest the presence of polariton modes. I recommend that the authors compute the first or second derivative of the signal with respect to energy (e.g., dI/dE or d2I/dE2), which is a widely used technique in the analysis of excitonic spectra. This approach could help reveal subtle features more clearly and provide stronger evidence for the existence of weak or overlapping polariton branches. 4. It would be helpful if the authors could provide the quality factor of their cavity. This parameter is essential for evaluating the cavity's optical performance and assessing whether the system operates in the strong coupling regime. Including this information would also facilitate comparison with previous studies. 5. In Fig. 2e, the authors present reflectance spectra at two different temperatures. Do the authors have data from a continuous temperature scan? Tracking the evolution of the polariton splitting as a function of temperature could provide additional evidence for the formation of polaritons. However, with only two temperature points shown, it is difficult to draw firm conclusions. A more comprehensive temperature-dependent analysis on a single device is encouraged. 6. In the optoelectronic measurements presented in Fig. 4, how do interfacial trap states between ITO and WS₂ affect the observed rise and response times? Given that exciton and polariton dynamics typically occur on picosecond to sub-nanosecond timescales, the reported response times on the order of hundreds of nanoseconds seem long (>> lifetime of exciton/polariton). This suggests that extrinsic effects, such as carrier trapping at the ITO/WS₂ interface, may play a significant role. The authors are encouraged to discuss the possible influence of interface quality and trap dynamics on the device performance.

### Reviewer 3

The manuscript reports a polariton photodiode in a self-hybridized TMD system and clarifies that some device performances, particularly the response time (up to hundreds of nanoseconds), could be enhanced in the strong coupling regime. The experimental data primarily support the interpretation of cavity effect of enhancement rather than one based on polaritons. Although there are some decent performance improvements, the main merit appears to lie in the fast response time, which is significantly faster than reported devices. While the performance improvements are noted, the enhancement mechanism in the so called “strong coupling regime “ remains unclear, and the demonstrated evidence is not convincing. Below are my detailed comments: 1) The novelty of polariton photodiode bring out some concerns. In the context of exciton polariton photodiodes, this idea has been tried several years ago in organic excitonic materials [e.g., ACS Photonics 5, 2921-2927 (2018)]. Though it may be an interesting attempt to realize this idea within TMDs, the experimental evidence in this manuscript is not yet sufficient to support polariton effects. Further data and clarification are required to substantiate the role of polaritons in the observed performance enhancement. 2) Insufficient evidence for the strong coupling regime. To claim the strong coupling regime, the coupling strengths were fitted under different detuning by varying the TMD thicknesses. This is problematic. The strong coupling can be verified by satisfying the criterion that the coupling strengths should be larger than the averaged linewidths of cavity modes and excitons. This means the g^2 should be greater than (gamma_c^2+gamma_x^2)/2. This criterion has not been tested in their spectroscopic measurements (Figs. 2a-b). The criterion in the SI they cited can only infer there could be spectral splitting, which does not necessarily indicate the strong coupling regime (please see many references discussing about the differences between the intermediate coupling and the strong coupling). It is also important to note that the guidelines do not exactly follow the reflectivity dips (Fig. 2b), which are misleading. 3) The coupling strengths is proportional to the sample thickness, which has been varied by more than 8 times. For a rough estimation without considering the detailed cavity mode distributions (which was also ignored in the manuscript), the coupling strengths in Fig. 2b could be varied by about 3 times. In this way, the so-called anti-crossing features in Figs. 2a-b is misleading, as they do not share similar cavity strengths. It should be appropriate to measure samples of the same thickness at different angles (angle-resolved reflectivity) and then extract the coupling strength specifically for each thickness. 4) In Fig. 2d, the authors claim that the normalized EQE data support the consistency of polariton resonances and EQE peaks. However, this is not the case in close observations. For example, some EQE peaks coincide with the exciton resonance instead of so called “LP” or “UP” states. To substantiate the polariton effect, it is strongly suggested that they should first clarify the well-separated polariton peaks by checking the criterion of the strong coupling regime, which are expected to be distant from the exciton resonances with respect to their linewidths. For instance, some convincing measurements should be at least performed in the “zero-detuning” samples to better determine the strong coupling regime. 5) In Fig. 2f, some error bars are excessively large, which are greater than the data variations. This largely undermines the reliability of the data and makes it difficult to draw convincing conclusions. The authors are strongly recommended to retake the data, and thus effectively reduce these error margins and provide more precise data to support their claims. 6) To strengthen the argument for a polariton-based photodiode, the correlation between the enhanced performances and the polariton states should be unambiguously established. In Figs 3, 4b, and 4d, the performance improvement in the device seems more likely to be due to cavity resonance rather than polariton formation. At the zero-detuning, the peak device performance coincides with the exact cavity resonance (in Fig. S9), indicating that cavity enhancement might be the optimized. This does not necessarily lead to polariton effects. To establish the polariton enhancements, demonstrating the optimized formation of polaritons and unambiguously identifying the peaks of performance parameters at the polariton states would be critical. 7) The comparisons with reported device performance seem to be suspicious. In their comparisons, the on/off ratio, dark current density, especially response time seems to be much larger than reported TMD-based photodiodes/photodetectors. However, there are some mistakes in SI that comparisons of device parameters with previously reported devices show several discrepancies. For instance, in SI Reference 20 [Adv. Electron. Mater. 7, 2000964 (2021)], the responsivity is given as 777 mA/W. But the manuscript lists it as 360 mA/W (SI Table S2). As another example, the responsivity in SI Reference 8 [Appl. Surf. Sci. 481, 1127-1132 (2019)] is reported to be about 5 orders of magnitude higher than this work. But the manuscript totally ignored it in the comparisons of responsivity (SI Table S2). The similar inconsistencies must be addressed and ensure all comparative data are correct and well-cited without such suspicious discrepancies. Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
Zhao et al. report their findings on exciton–polariton photodiodes constructed from
ITO/multilayer WS /Au structures and present measurements of several key
2
optoelectronic parameters—including EQE, IQE, responsivity, and rise time—all of
which exhibit peak values at a thickness corresponding to the emergence of possible
polariton modes. The characterization of the devices is thorough, and the results
demonstrate a high degree of internal consistency. However, attributing the observed
phenomena to polaritons does not appear to be fully convincing, as some of the reported
properties are not consistent with typical polariton behavior. In my view, the manuscript
would benefit from further clarification and supporting evidence before it can be
considered suitable for publication.
Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for their thoughtful and thorough evaluation of our
manuscript. We greatly appreciate the positive comments on the quality of device
fabrication, the comprehensive characterization, and the internal consistency of the
results. Your critical feedback, particularly regarding the attribution of our results to
exciton-polariton modes, has been extremely valuable in helping us refine our
interpretations and improve the clarity and rigor of the manuscript.
In response, we have carefully addressed each of your concerns and revised the
manuscript accordingly. Below, we provide detailed responses to each specific point,
including additional clarifications and supporting evidence. We hope that the revised
version meets your expectations and more clearly conveys the significance of our
findings.
1. In Fig 2a and 2b, the authors present the simulated and measured polariton modes
for different WS thicknesses. They report an increase in the vacuum Rabi splitting with
2
increasing WS thickness. However, this trend raises several concerns. First, as the
2
thickness of the WS layer increases, the mode volume V of the cavity is expected to
2
increase. Since the light-matter coupling strength 𝑔 scales inversely with the square
root of the mode volume (𝑔 ∝ 1/√𝑉), a larger mode volume should lead to a decrease
in 𝑔, and thus a smaller Rabi splitting. Second, the exciton oscillator strength typically
decreases in thicker flakes due to enhanced dielectric screening and a weakening of the
direct K-K transition in WS . Therefore, one would also expect a reduction in 𝑔 with
2
increasing thickness. These considerations appear inconsistent with the observed trend
and should be clarified by the authors.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for raising this important and insightful question. While the
intuitive picture is that a larger mode volume weakens the coupling strength, in our case
multiple cooperative effects, such as the increased number of excitons participating in
the interaction and the improved overlap with the optical field, work together to
reinforce the coupling, leading to the observed enhancement in vacuum Rabi splitting.
Specifically:
(1) Cooperative scaling of mode volume (V ) and exciton number (N):
Indeed, it is correct in principle that, for a fixed number of excitons N, an increase in
the mode volume V leads to a reduction in the light-matter coupling strength, as
described by the relation:

This cooperative scaling has been discussed in prior studies (e.g., Nat. Mater. 22,
970-976 (2023); Nat. Commun. 13, 5597 (2022); Phys. Rev. B 107, 075415(2023)) and
is particularly relevant in systems like ours where a bare cavity is absent and the field
is concentrated within the absorbing medium itself.
Furthermore, consistent physical behavior has been observed in multilayer TMDs
systems, as demonstrated in plasmonic systems (ACS Photonics 6, 286 (2019); Nano
Lett. 21, 605 (2021); Nanophotonics 12, 3267 (2023)), bloch surface wave platforms
(ACS Photonics 9, 2817 (2022)). These works establish the same quantitative scaling

2. Continuing from the previous point, the authors report a vacuum Rabi splitting of
approximately 170 meV. However, even in optimized systems where monolayer WS
2
(or other TMDCs) is strongly coupled to a planar cavity, the vacuum Rabi splitting
typically falls in the range of 40-60 meV (e.g. Nature Nano 17, 396-402 2022). In
contrast, the authors observe a Rabi splitting that is nearly four times larger than these
established values, despite using thicker WS flakes, which generally exhibit reduced
2
oscillator strength. This reported value appears unphysically large given the material
system and cavity architecture, and the authors should provide further justification or
supporting analysis to clarify this discrepancy.
Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for this important and insightful point. We confirm that
the large vacuum Rabi splitting of ~170 meV observed in our system is physically
reasonable and consistent with both theory and recent literature. Although this value
exceeds the typical 40-60 meV reported for monolayer TMDC-cavity systems, it is
attributed to enhanced collective coupling of exciton in our multilayer self-
hybridized geometry. Specifically:
1) Key differences from monolayer-cavity systems:
We agree that monolayer WS exhibits a higher per-exciton oscillator strength
2
compared to bulk flakes. However, the total light-matter coupling strength 𝑔, and
consequently the vacuum Rabi splitting, is determined not only by the oscillator
strength per exciton but also by the total number of participating excitons 𝑁, and
the optical mode volume 𝑉. This relationship is well established in the literature
(e.g., Refs. [Nat. Mater. 22, 970–976 (2023); Phys. Rev. B 107, 075415; Nat.
Commun. 13, 5597 (2022)]) following the relation:
𝑁
𝑔 ∝ √
𝑉
In monolayer-based systems, despite the strong oscillator strength of a single
exciton, the number of available emitters N is extremely limited due to the atomic
thickness of the film. In contrast, in our system, the cavity is self-hybridized and
composed of multilayer WS , with thicknesses >50 nm, placing the system well into
2
the quasi-bulk regime. While the per-exciton oscillator strength may be lower, the
number of participating excitons is significantly greater.
In this structure, the exciton number 𝑁 is significantly higher than that of the
monolayer-based system. Meanwhile, the cavity mode volume 𝑉 does not increase
significantly compared with the conventional Fabry-Pérot cavity. Therefore, the
overall coupling strength is significantly enhanced. This structure leads us to
observe a vacuum Rabi splitting of approximately 170 meV, which is a
manifestation of enhanced exciton collective coupling in thick-layer TMDC
systems (see Table R2.2).
2) Literature precedent for large Rabi splitting in thick TMDC systems:
Our observation of a ~170 meV vacuum Rabi splitting is consistent with recent
studies on self-hybridized polaritonic systems involving thick TMDC films.
Notably, Munkhbat et al. (ACS Photonics 6, 139-147, 2019) and others (Phys. Rev.
B 107, 075415, 2023; Nat. Commun. 13, 5597, 2022) have reported that strong
collective coupling in such systems can lead to significantly enhanced Rabi splitting,
often exceeding those of monolayer-based systems.
These findings confirm that large Rabi splitting in the >100 meV range is
physically reasonable and achievable in TMDC systems with similar architectures.
3) Extraction of Rabi splitting:
To ensure the reliability of the extracted Rabi splitting, we performed new angle-
resolved reflectivity spectra and fitted the polariton dispersion using a standard
coupled oscillator model. Both the upper and lower polariton branches were well
reproduced by the model (see Fig. R2.3). The extracted Rabi splitting is 151.4 meV,
178.8 meV, and 186.1 meV, respectively (see Table R2.2).
This consistency between experimental observation and theoretical modeling
further supports the physical validity of the large Rabi splitting reported in our work.

4. It would be helpful if the authors could provide the quality factor of their cavity. This
parameter is essential for evaluating the cavity's optical performance and assessing
whether the system operates in the strong coupling regime. Including this information
would also facilitate comparison with previous studies.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. The cavity quality factors were
extracted from the linewidths of the cavity modes in the wavelength domain.
Specifically, the full width at half maximum (FWHM) of each cavity resonance, Δλ,
was obtained and converted into the quality factor using Q=λ /Δλ, where λ is the
0 0
resonance wavelength. We calculate this from TMM at a λ of 800 nm (off resonance)
0
for each cavity mode. This procedure yields approximate Q values of 16, 20, and 25 for
the first-, second-, and third-order modes, respectively.
These quality factors are reasonable for self-hybridized cavity systems and are
sufficient to support the formation of polariton states. This conclusion is further
supported by the linewidths analyzed in the energy domain, where the measured
vacuum Rabi splitting significantly exceeds the combined cavity and exciton linewidths,
thereby fulfilling the strong coupling criterion. For self-hybridized cavities, future work
will need to focus on strategies such as optimizing material interface quality, employing
lower-loss active materials, or engineering photonic structures with better in-plane
confinement to further enhance the quality factor.
Revised:
We have now included the above information regarding the cavity Q factors in the
revised manuscript (see Supplementary Information, Page 5).

temperature dependence of polaritonic behavior, we conducted continuous
temperature-dependent reflectance measurements (from 87 K to 300 K) on several WS

We thank the reviewer for raising this important point regarding the difference between
the intrinsic exciton/polariton dynamics and the device-level response time observed in
Fig. 4. To clarify this issue, we conducted a series of additional experiments to evaluate
the influence of interfacial trap states and extrinsic defects on both exciton lifetime and
photoresponse dynamics.
Indeed, while exciton and polariton lifetimes typically lie in the picosecond–sub-
nanosecond regime, the observed rise and response time in Fig. 4 are longer (hundreds
of nanoseconds), indicating the presence of extrinsic limiting mechanisms. The rise and
fall times in photodetectors are generally governed not only by the intrinsic
exciton/polariton dynamics but also by carrier trapping and detrapping at
interfaces and surfaces, as well as carrier transport within the device channel.
These defect states are inevitably introduced during device fabrication.
To investigate the influence of interfacial defect states on the lifetime of
exciton/polariton and response time of exciton-polariton devices, we prepared two
devices from the same nanosheet (Fig. R2.8d): pristine WS nanosheets obtained by
2
mechanical exfoliation, and the same WS nanosheets subjected to 23 s of oxygen
2
plasma treatment, emulating the defect formation typically induced during ITO
sputtering. The surface morphology was examined using atomic force microscopy
(AFM) (Fig. R2.8). The WS thickness was measured to be 79.9 nm (Fig. R2.8a). Root-
2
mean-square (r.m.s.) roughness analysis revealed that the pristine WS nanosheet
2
exhibited an atomically clean surface with an r.m.s. roughness of 0.31 nm (Fig. R2.8
fb). After O plasma treatment, the r.m.s. roughness increased to 1.02 nm (Fig. R2.8
2
fc), indicating surface degradation and the formation of uniformly distributed defects.
The rise and response times of a photodetector are fundamentally governed by
intrinsic material dynamics. Although the lifetimes of excitons and polaritons typically
lie in the picosecond-to-sub-nanosecond range, interfacial carrier trapping at the
ITO/WS interface and the subsequent slow release of trapped carriers can prolong
2
the overall photocurrent response. In our case, plasma treatment increases the density
of interfacial trap states, which accelerates recombination (shortening the
exciton/polariton lifetime (Fig. R2.8e)) while simultaneously slowing net carrier
extraction and transport due to transient trapping-detrapping dynamics. These trap
states delay carrier collection and extend the photocurrent response into the
nanosecond regime, consistent with the features observed in Fig. R2.8 f. Nevertheless,
the response times of our devices remain much faster than those of most other excitonic
photodetectors (main text, Fig.4f).
Although the response speed is still below the theoretical limit owing to the group
velocity of polaritons, our additional data strengthen the validity of the results and
highlight the promise of this approach for future studies. Future research should focus
on reducing carrier trapping at the ITO/WS interface and optimizing the relaxation
2
dynamics of exciton/polaritonic states, such as suppressing non-radiative losses,
extending lifetimes, and promoting rapid energy transfer, to further enhance the
generation and transport efficiency of photogenerated carriers. Potential strategies to
mitigate interfacial defects include adopting physical transfer of electrodes to avoid
plasma-induced damage, introducing ultrathin interfacial passivation layers,
employing van der Waals contacts, or using chemical surface treatments to reduce
trap density. Such improvements are expected to markedly shorten the rise time of the
photoresponse, which is particularly critical for the development of sub-nanosecond,
fast photodiodes for applications in optical communication and sensing. These
improvements are expected to fully unlock the potential of polariton-enhanced
transport in next-generation optoelectronic devices and shorten the rise time of the
photoresponse, which is particularly critical for the development of sub-nanosecond,
fast photodiodes for optical communication and sensing applications.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
The manuscript reports a polariton photodiode in a self-hybridized TMD system and
clarifies that some device performances, particularly the response time (up to hundreds
of nanoseconds), could be enhanced in the strong coupling regime. The experimental
data primarily support the interpretation of cavity effect of enhancement rather than one
based on polaritons. Although there are some decent performance improvements, the
main merit appears to lie in the fast response time, which is significantly faster than
reported devices. While the performance improvements are noted, the enhancement
mechanism in the so called “strong coupling regime” remains unclear, and the
demonstrated evidence is not convincing. Below are my detailed comments:
Response:
We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful and critical evaluation of our manuscript. We
sincerely appreciate the recognition of the fast response time and performance
improvements in our polariton photodiodes. We understand the reviewer’s concern
regarding the attribution of device enhancements to strong light-matter coupling rather
than purely to cavity effects. In the revised manuscript, we have taken substantial steps
to clarify the physical mechanisms underlying the observed enhancements and to
further distinguish the role of polaritonic modes from conventional cavity-induced
effects. We would also like to point out that while evidence of polaritons in the
optoelectronic responses in these devices is clear, the true merit in terms of performance
(response speed) is still far from theoretical values due to imperfect materials and
interfaces. Optimization of materials and related interfaces is beyond the scope of
current work and will be part of future efforts.
We have expanded our analysis to include:
a) Temperature-dependent reflectance spectra (87-300 K), which
demonstrate continuous, non-collapsing mode splitting consistent with
polariton branches rather than Fabry-Pérot resonances (see revised Fig. 2e and
Supplementary Fig. S13).
b) Angle-resolved dispersion mapping and coupled oscillator model
fitting, producing Rabi splitting values that are reproducible and consistent
across several independent experimental methods, further confirming the
presence of strong coupling (see revised Supplementary Fig. S6).
c) The relationship between reflectance spectra and EQE demonstrates
photoresponse and quantum efficiency enhancements that correlate well with
the dispersion of polariton modes (see revised Fig. 2c).
These revisions are described in detail in our responses to the specific comments
below, and the corresponding modifications have been incorporated throughout the
manuscript. We hope these additions provide a clearer picture of how the strong
coupling between excitons and photons contributes to the observed optoelectronic
performance enhancements.
1) The novelty of polariton photodiode bring out some concerns. In the context of
exciton polariton photodiodes, this idea has been tried several years ago in organic
excitonic materials [e.g., ACS Photonics 5, 2921-2927 (2018)]. Though it may be an
interesting attempt to realize this idea within TMDs, the experimental evidence in this
manuscript is not yet sufficient to support polariton effects. Further data and
clarification are required to substantiate the role of polaritons in the observed
performance enhancement.
Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for acknowledging our effort to explore polariton
photodiodes within the TMD material system. We appreciate the reference to prior work
on organic excitonic materials, such as ACS Photonics 5, 2921-2927 (2018), which
indeed laid important groundwork in this area.
While the concept of exciton-polariton photodetectors has been previously
demonstrated in organic systems, our work presents a fundamentally distinct strategy.
It is also worth noting that organic excitonic semiconductors cannot achieve self-
hybridization due to low values of real part of refractive indices and therefore always
have to rely on closed Fabry-Perot cavity systems. Further the
nanocrystalline/amorphous nature of organic semiconductors obfuscates the transport
of excitons. In contrast WS has high real part of refractive index and exciton transport
2
is highly anisotropic in v.s. out of plane making it a much better model system for
investigating polariton and strong coupling effects in photodiode and photovoltaic
devices.
As shown in Figure R3.1, unlike metal-mirror organic polariton photodiodes that rely
on a closed Fabry-Pérot cavity (ACS Photonics 5, 2921-2927 (2018)) and whose
internal quantum efficiency is limited by Ag electrode losses, our device realizes
cavity-free self-hybridized (our work) polaritons in multilayer WS , where a single
architecture not only yields dispersive, thickness-quantized polaritons whose extrema
align with EQE/IQE oscillations and near-unity IQE at zero detuning but also delivers
device-level advantages, high responsivity (~ 0.35 A/W), low NEP (~0.34 pW Hz-
1/2), and sub-μs response (~217 ns), which were not accessible in previous
demonstrations (ACS Photonics 5, 2921-2927 (2018)).

3) Link to device performance (Reflectance ↔ EQE):
Finally, we explicitly correlate the polariton dispersion with device-level
metrics by showing that the enhancements in EQE spectra occur at energies that
coincide with the polariton branches (Fig. 2c-d; see also Fig. R3.5). Figure
R3.5a shows the coupled oscillator model fit, along with the experimental EQE
peak wavelengths extracted from a range of device thicknesses. Notably, the
peak response positions of the EQE spectra in devices with varying thicknesses
(scattered dots) exhibit excellent agreement with the theoretical model (dashed
lines). In particular, the evolution of their wavelength positions with thickness
strictly follows the characteristic dispersion relation of polaritons, with the peak
positions corresponding to the resonance modes of the UP and LP branches,
respectively. This consistency between experimental observations and the
theoretical model provides solid evidence that the polariton state enhances light-
trapping efficiency by modulating photon-exciton interactions, clearly
demonstrating the crucial role of polariton engineering in improving photodiode
performance. Figure R3.5b shows the EQE spectra of three representative
devices, one in the weak coupling regime, one near zero detuning for the first
order polariton, and one near zero detuning for the second order polariton. In
these strongly coupled devices, both the lower polariton branch (LPB) and
upper polariton branch (UPB) exhibit spectral separations from the bare exciton
resonance that exceed their respective linewidths. This clear spectral separation
enables unambiguous identification of the polariton branches. The responses
below the bare exciton energy of the strongly coupled devices can be observed,
and the peaks of the responses correspond to the reflectance minima (attributed
to UP and LP branches) reported in the Fig.R3.5c. These features are absent in
weakly coupled devices, confirming that all these responses are dominated by
the E-P states. This direct correspondence between optical dispersion and
photoresponse provides strong evidence that the observed performance
enhancements stem from polariton-assisted absorption and transport, rather
than from conventional cavity effects.

4) In Fig. 2d, the authors claim that the normalized EQE data support the consistency
of polariton resonances and EQE peaks. However, this is not the case in close
observations. For example, some EQE peaks coincide with the exciton resonance
instead of so called “LP” or “UP” states. To substantiate the polariton effect, it is

Response:
We appreciate the reviewer’s observation and agree that a rigorous assignment of EQE
peaks to polariton modes requires verification of both the strong coupling regime and
sufficient spectral separation between the polariton branches and the bare exciton.
We confirm that the observed EQE peaks indeed originate from polariton resonances rather
than bare excitonic absorption. To rigorously establish this assignment, we have
reanalyzed the data with stricter strong coupling criteria and carried out additional
measurements on zero-detuning devices.
1) Verification of strong coupling regime:
To strengthen our analysis, we performed further measurements on additional
devices and collected angle-resolved reflectivity spectra, which were then fitted
using a coupled oscillator model to precisely identify the LP and UP states. We
applied established strong coupling criteria to all measured devices, retaining only

2) Zero-detuning devices as direct evidence:
In detuned cavities, one polariton branch may naturally converge toward the
exciton resonance, which explains the occasional coincidence of EQE peaks with
the exciton energy.
To directly confirm the strong coupling regime, we fabricated and characterized
representative zero-detuning samples (77.9 nm, 151.2 nm). For these devices, we
performed angle-resolved reflectance and reflectance intensity spectra together
with the corresponding EQE data (Fig. R3.9).
WS devices with thicknesses of 77.9 nm and 151.2 nm correspond closely to
2
the zero-detuning conditions for the first- and second-order cavity modes,
respectively. In their angle-resolved reflectance spectra, we observe clear
anticrossing behavior (Fig. R3.9a, b), indicative of hybrid exciton-photon states
formed under strong coupling. These spectral splittings reflect the self-
hybridization of excitons with cavity modes, and the measured dispersions are well
reproduced by the coupled oscillator model. The extracted coupling strengths (82.5
meV and 93.2 meV) satisfy both established strong coupling criteria, confirming
the robustness of the exciton-photon interaction.
Reflectance intensity spectra further reveal two distinct absorption peaks on
either side of the A-exciton resonance for the strongly coupled devices (151.2 nm
and 77.9 nm), in excellent agreement with the predicted lower and upper polariton
branches (Fig. R3.9c). By contrast, weakly coupled devices (39.6 nm) exhibit only
a single excitonic feature (Fig. R3.9c).
Consistently, the EQE spectra of zero-detuning devices display well-separated
responses from the LPB and UPB, with splitting that exceed their respective
linewidths (Fig. R3.9d). These EQE peaks correspond directly to the reflectance
minima associated with the polariton branches (Fig. R3.9c). The responses below
the bare exciton energy of the strongly coupled devices can be observed. Such
features are absent in weakly coupled devices (Fig. R3.9c, d; device of 39.6 nm),
providing direct evidence that the observed photocurrent originates from exciton-
photon hybrid (E-P) states.

6) To strengthen the argument for a polariton-based photodiode, the correlation
between the enhanced performances and the polariton states should be unambiguously
established. In Figs 3, 4b, and 4d, the performance improvement in the device seems
more likely to be due to cavity resonance rather than polariton formation. At the zero-
detuning, the peak device performance coincides with the exact cavity resonance (in
Fig. S9), indicating that cavity enhancement might be the optimized. This does not
necessarily lead to polariton effects. To establish the polariton enhancements,
demonstrating the optimized formation of polaritons and unambiguously identifying
the peaks of performance parameters at the polariton states would be critical.
Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the insightful comment regarding the need to
unambiguously establish the correlation between enhanced device performance and
polariton states. We fully agree that distinguishing between cavity resonance effects and
polariton formation is critical to strengthen the argument for a polariton photodiode.
While cavity resonances can indeed enhance the local optical field, our data
demonstrate that strong exciton-photon coupling leads to polariton states whose
influence extends beyond what is expected from bare cavity effects alone. Finally, we
would also like to point out that while evidence of polaritons in the optoelectronic
responses in these devices is clear, the true merit in terms of performance (response
speed) is still far from theoretical values due to imperfect materials and interfaces.
Optimization of materials and related interfaces is beyond the scope of current work
and will be part of future efforts.
Below we address the reviewer’s concerns with additional evidence supporting the
polaritonic origin of the enhancements.
1) Zero-detuning devices provide unambiguous evidence.
In the absence of strong coupling, cavity resonance enhances only a single optical
mode without splitting, leading merely to a strengthened resonance peak (Fig.
R3.13 c,d; device of 39.6 nm). By contrast, exciton-polariton formation results
in the emergence of distinct lower and upper polariton branches (LP/UP)
separated by a Rabi splitting (Fig. R3.13 c,d; device of 77.9 nm and 151.2 nm).
In representative zero-detuning devices (e.g. WS thicknesses of 77.9 nm and
2
151.2 nm, corresponding approximately to the first- and second-order maxima ),
the LP/UP are well resolved (see Fig.R3.13a,b) and the reflectance minima
(polariton modes, see Fig.R3.13c) show a one-to-one correspondence with EQE
maxima (see Fig.R3.4 d) , confirming that the photoresponse in these devices is
dominated by exciton-polariton states. The extracted couplings (≈92 and 93.5
meV) satisfy the strong coupling criteria. Owing to exciton-polariton formation,
strongly coupled devices can harvest more photons in the spectral region near the
bandgap. Compared with conventional cavity resonance, this approach avoids the
narrowband absorption inherent to cavity enhancement and the limitation of high
absorption efficiency only at specific wavelengths. As a result, both the cut-off
wavelength is extended, and near-unity internal quantum efficiency is achieved
for on-resonance devices (see Fig.R3.13d). The observed performance
enhancement in these devices cannot be explained by a single uncoupled cavity
mode.

Reviewer #2 (Comments to the Author):
The authors have adequately addressed my previous concerns regarding the size of the
vacuum Rabi splitting, the Q value of the cavity mode, and the clarity of the observed
anti-crossing. They have also provided a detailed discussion on the influence of trap
states on device performance. Overall, I find that the revised manuscript meets the
standard for publication.
I do have one remaining question regarding the temperature-dependent polariton
branches. The splitting appears to persist up to room temperature. Could the authors
clarify the physical origin of this robustness?
Response:
We sincerely appreciate your review of our response letter and revised manuscript, as
well as your positive evaluation of our work. We are delighted to learn that the revisions
and supplementary discussions addressing all your earlier concerns, including the
magnitude of the vacuum Rabi splitting, the Q factor of the cavity mode, the clarity of
the anti-crossing behavior, and the influence of trap states on device performance, have
been met with your approval. Your insightful comments have been invaluable in
enhancing the overall quality of our manuscript. We are also very pleased that you
consider the current version of our manuscript to meet the standard for publication.
Regarding your question on the temperature-dependent polariton branches and the
persistence of the splitting up to room temperature, the robustness originates primarily
from the large exciton binding energy in our material system. Two-dimensional (2D)
transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) such as WS exhibit reduced dielectric
2
screening and strong quantum confinement effects, leading to exceptionally large
exciton binding energies (>300 meV) in monolayer materials, while the interlayer van
der Waals interactions also ensure binding energies greater than the thermal energy at
room temperature (~25 meV) even in bulk or multilayer forms. [ref: Phys. Rev. Lett.,
2014, 113(7), 76802；Nat. Commun., 2016, 7, 10643.] This high binding energy
prevents thermal dissociation of excitons, maintaining coupling with the cavity photons
even as temperature increases. Additionally, the vacuum Rabi splitting (Ω ≈ 180 meV)
is much larger than both the thermal broadening and the homogeneous linewidths of
the excitons and cavity mode, ensuring that the anti-crossing remains resolvable.
Therefore, the large exciton binding energy, strong exciton-photon coupling, and
substantial Rabi splitting collectively ensure that the polariton branches remain clearly
resolved and the splitting persists up to room temperature.
Reviewer #3 (Comments to the Author):
We appreciate the authors’ efforts to address our previous concerns in the last report.
The manuscript has been indeed improved from the earlier version. The authors have
seriously looked into the polaritonic effects and carefully examined the criterion of the

to the correlations between the polaritonic resonances and maxima of the device
performance measures. These points are critical to check the technical correctness of
their claim. However, we still have several concerns for these technical points as well
as the novelty of this work before it can be considered for publication. Here are our
detailed comments as below.
Response:
We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful and constructive feedback. We are
pleased to know that the improvements in the revised manuscript have been recognized,
especially regarding the identification of polaritonic effects, the verification of the
strong coupling regime, and the correlation between the polariton resonances and the
device performance. We would like to once again express our gratitude for these
insightful comments and suggestions, which have not only helped us produce a
substantially improved manuscript but also motivated us to conduct a deeper
investigation into the underlying physics.
We have carefully addressed all remaining concerns regarding both the technical
correctness and the novelty of our work. In this revised version, we have further
clarified the physical mechanisms, added new supporting analyses, and strengthened
the presentation of experimental evidence to ensure that our claims are technically
sound and well justified. Detailed point-by-point responses are provided below.
1) In comparison with previous similar work [e.g., ACS Photonics 5, 2921-2927 (2018)],
the authors claimed the novelty lies on the self-hybridized polaritons for the
photodiodes, broadband absorption, polariton-enabled transport and improved device
performance. The concept of self-hybridized exciton polaritons is not new, and does not
seem to play a significant role in the device performance (actually it might introduce
some intrinsic limits for the device performance), which has also been pointed out by
the other reviewer. However, the polariton-enabled transport seems to be a quite
interesting point, which is actually an important topic for the polaritonics [e.g., Nat
Mater 2015, 14, 1123-1129]. Moreover, the polariton-mediated Purcell effect could be
also some interesting point for boosting optoelectronic device performance, which
might be related with this work [e.g., Nature 2024, 626, 300-306]. The authors are
suggested to find some more significant points to support the claimed novelty.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for their constructive feedback and for highlighting the
interesting aspects of polariton-enabled transport in our work. We appreciate the
suggestion to further emphasize the novelty by identifying additional significant points.
Below, we address the reviewer’s concerns point by point, clarifying how our study
advances beyond prior work while building on established concepts in polaritonics.
First, regarding the comparison to previous similar work (e.g., ACS Photonics 5,
2921-2927 (2018), hereafter Ref. 31 in our manuscript), we agree that strong light-
matter coupling has been explored in organic photodiodes to extend spectral
responsivity. However, that study relied on external optical cavities with partially
transparent metal reflectors, which introduced energy losses and limited device
performance. In contrast, our work demonstrates the integration of self-hybridized
exciton-polaritons into an inorganic excitonic photodiode (using WS ) without
2
external cavities, leveraging the material’s intrinsic high refractive index for self-
trapping and hybridization of light. This eliminates the need for lossy reflectors,
enabling broadband absorption across 500-800 nm while achieving near-unity
internal quantum efficiency (IQE > 90%) near zero detuning, performance metrics
that outperform those in Ref. 31(EQE <15%; IQE < 25%) and related organic systems.
We have revised the introduction and discussion sections to more explicitly contrast
these architectural differences, emphasizing how our open-cavity approach (inspired by
recent advances, e.g., Refs. 34-35) avoids the trade-offs in prior designs.
While the concept of self-hybridized exciton-polaritons is indeed not new (as
demonstrated before in multilayer TMDCs), its application here plays an important role
in device performance. In our devices, self-hybridization enables strong photon-
exciton coupling directly within the WS absorber, resulting in observable anti-
2
crossing in thickness-dependent reflectance and external quantum efficiency (EQE)
spectra, with Rabi splittings of 152-173 meV. This directly contributes to enhanced
sub-bandgap absorption via the lower polariton branch (LPB), extending the cut-off
wavelength (Supplementary Fig. S11) without compromising broadband response.
Critically, it facilitates polariton-enhanced transport, leading to oscillatory IQE
behavior with thickness and peaks at zero-detuning points (≈75 nm and 145 nm for
l=1,2 modes), approaching unity IQE, suggesting improved exciton diffusion lengths
that mitigate recombination losses in conventional excitonic photodiodes. The self-
hybridized state appears to alleviate the narrow-band absorption and short diffusion
length typically associated with excitonic semiconductors such as WS . To address the
2
reviewer’s point, we have added a discussion in the main text (Device structure and
working principle section) on potential limitations, such as imperfect interfaces
affecting response speed (e.g., interfacial carrier trapping, Supplementary Fig. S20),
and how material optimizations could further elevate performance toward theoretical
polaritonic limits.
We fully concur that polariton-enabled transport is a key novelty and an important
topic in polaritonics, as noted in the reference (Nat. Mater. 2015, 14, 1123–1129; now
cited as Ref. 47 in the revised manuscript). Our study provides direct experimental
evidence of this in a functional photodiode, where strong coupling enhances exciton
transport via photonic modes, yielding a minimum response time of 217 ns—faster than
reportedroom-temperature excitonic photodetectors (Supplementary Table 3). This is
supported by our phenomenological transport model (Supplementary Fig. S14), which
aligns with experimental IQE trends and attributes oscillations to resonance energy
transfer weighted by the polariton’s excitonic fraction. Unlike prior demonstrations
focused on fundamental transport (e.g., long-range propagation in monolayers, Refs.
23-24), our work integrates this into a device architecture, demonstrating a 20-fold EQE
increase entering the strong-coupling regime and a -3 dB cutoff frequency of 1.21 MHz.
Additionally, we appreciate the suggestion regarding the polariton-mediated Purcell
effect (e.g., Nature 2024, 626, 300-306; now cited as a new reference 54 in the
discussion), which can facilitate more efficient charge separation and suppressed non-
radiative recombination. While our primary focus is on transport enhancement,
polaritonic effects may indeed contribute to modified radiative rates, potentially
boosting charge separation at interfaces. Our low-temperature EQE data (Fig. 2e-f)
show preserved polaritonic features and enhanced efficiency, consistent with
suppressed non-radiative recombination, aligning with Purcell-like modifications.
We have added a brief discussion in the EQE section to explore this connection, noting a
direction for future studies to quantitatively evaluate this effect.
We hope these revisions incorporate the reviewer’s suggested references and enhance
the manuscript’s clarity on novelty. We believe they address the concerns and strengthen
the paper’s impact.

In the revised manuscript, we have expanded the Introduction and Discussion
sections to better clarify the novelty of our cavity-free, self-hybridized polariton
photodiode compared with previously reported cavity-based systems (see pages 2 and
8 of the main text). Specifically, we emphasize that the transparent top electrode
simultaneously serves as an antireflective layer, enabling strong light–matter
coupling in an open-cavity architecture with broadband absorption and polariton-
enhanced transport.
In the Device structure and working principle section (page 3), we have incorporated
a discussion on extrinsic performance limitations—including interfacial trap states,

2) For the tests of the strong coupling regime, there are still some points that should be
carefully examined. First, the thickness-dependent coupling strength seems to be quite
complicated. For the same cavity conditions, the coupling strength scales with the
square-root of the thickness. For example, the thicknesses between 150-180 nm seem
to host the similar l=2 cavity mode (Fig. R3.5a). In Table R3.2, the coupling strength
for the thicknesses between 150 nm and 180 nm does not really follow this scaling law.
This causes some confusion. Second, how did the authors determine the cavity
linewidths? The linewidths are so broad and even broader than the exciton linewidths.
For higher-order cavity modes, the linewidths generally should become narrower. The
fitted cavity linewidths do not really follow this trend. Third, how did the authors
determine the exciton linewidths. As the authors mentioned in the response, the
oscillator strength of the excitons should become constant for the bulk thickness (the
reference of Nature Photon 2015 is irrelevant with their argument there). For this
scenario, the exciton linewidths should be also taken as a constant and independent of
the bulk thickness. In Table R3.2, this does not seem to be the case.
Response:
We appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful comments on the strong coupling analysis.
Below we clarify the physical reasoning and methodological details regarding the
coupling strength, linewidth determination, and their thickness dependence.
(1) Thickness dependence of coupling strength.
In principle, when the optical mode volume 𝑉 remains approximately constant,
an increase in the number of excitons 𝑁 enhances the overall exciton-photon
interaction strength, following the relation
𝑁
𝑔 ∝ √
𝑉
However, in our self-hybridized system, the number of emitters (𝑵) exhibits an
approximately linear increase with thickness, while the optical mode volume (𝑽)
also expands with increasing thickness. As a result, the overall coupling strength
(𝑔) varies only slightly over a wide thickness range, which is consistent with our
experimental observations. Therefore, the observed Rabi splitting in our structures
reflects a balance between the increased exciton density and the enlarged mode
volume. This interplay between 𝑁 and 𝑉 has been well established in the literature
on self-hybridized and collective light-matter coupling systems [Nat. Mater. 22,
970–976 (2023); Phys. Rev. B 107, 075415 (2023); Nat. Commun. 13, 5597 (2022)].
(2) Determination of cavity linewidths.
The cavity linewidths are extracted by fitting the reflectance of each cavity
mode at large detuning, where exciton-photon interaction is minimal. These
linewidths serve as the initial inputs for the thickness-dependent fits and are allowed
to vary slightly to achieve the best fit. The relatively broad linewidths arise from
the intrinsic optical dissipation and imperfect optical confinement in the WS layers,
2
which is typical for self-hybridized cavity systems and still sufficient to sustain
polaritonic states. Moreover, the measured vacuum Rabi splitting exceeds the
combined linewidths of the exciton and cavity modes, satisfying the strong-
coupling criterion. Future improvements in interface quality and in-plane
confinement are expected to further enhance the cavity Q-factor.
(3) Determination of exciton linewidths.
The exciton linewidths are obtained by fitting a Lorentz oscillator to the
imaginary part of the dielectric function around the A-exciton resonance. The
fitting is performed over a narrow spectral range on the high-energy side to avoid
the influence of overlapping absorption tails. The extracted linewidths show only
small fluctuations across different thicknesses, mainly due to experimental and
fitting uncertainties, while the intrinsic exciton linewidth remains essentially
constant, consistent with the expected bulk-like behavior.
(4) Clarifications in angle-dependent fitting.
Following the reviewer’s suggestion, we have refined the angle-dependent fitting
procedure (Fig.R3.1 and Table R3.1): (i) the exciton linewidths are now fixed to
the constant values extracted from the dielectric function, and (ii) the cavity
linewidths are fixed to those obtained from thickness-dependent fitting. Only the
coupling strength and parameters related to cavity dispersion are allowed to vary.
This ensures consistency and reduces the number of fitting parameters.
(5) Regarding the reference Nature Photon. 9, 466-470 (2015):
We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. The reference to Nature Photonics 9,
466-470 (2015) was not intended to directly support the thickness dependence of
the oscillator strength, but rather to provide quantitative information on the exciton
Bohr radius (~1 nm) in WS . This small Bohr radius indicates that the exciton
2
wavefunction is highly localized within a single layer, implying that the oscillator
strength becomes nearly independent of thickness once the film exceeds a few
layers. We apologize for the confusion regarding the relevance of this reference.

Reviewer #3 (Comments to the Author):
The authors have adequately addressed most of my previous comments.
Before recommending publication, I have one final suggestion regarding the framing
of the work. The use of self-hybridized polaritons in an open cavity is presented as a
practical approach for device applications. However, the relatively high refractive index
of TMDs results in an intrinsically moderate quality factor for such open cavities. While
this configuration demonstrates polariton effects, applications generally require cavities
with higher quality factors and smaller mode volumes for optimal performance. If

performance could be significantly improved through the careful design of an integrated

and for acknowledging that most of the previous comments have been satisfactorily

### Reviewer 1

The authors have addressed all of the concerns raised, and I believe the paper is now suitable for acceptance in its current form.

### Reviewer 2

The authors have adequately addressed my previous concerns regarding the size of the vacuum Rabi splitting, the Q value of the cavity mode, and the clarity of the observed anti-crossing. They have also provided a detailed discussion on the influence of trap states on device performance. Overall, I find that the revised manuscript meets the standard for publication. I do have one remaining question regarding the temperature-dependent polariton branches. The splitting appears to persist up to room temperature. Could the authors clarify the physical origin of this robustness?

### Reviewer 3

We appreciate the authors’ efforts to address our previous concerns in the last report. The manuscript has been indeed improved from the earlier version. The authors have seriously looked into the polaritonic effects and carefully examined the criterion of the strong coupling regime. More importantly, the authors have paid substantial attentions to the correlations between the polaritonic resonances and maxima of the device performance measures. These points are critical to check the technical correctness of their claim. However, we still have several concerns for these technical points as well as the novelty of this work before it can be considered for publication. Here are our detailed comments as below. 1) In comparison with previous similar work [e.g., ACS Photonics 5, 2921-2927 (2018)], the authors claimed the novelty lies on the self-hybridized polaritons for the photodiodes, broadband absorption, polariton-enabled transport and improved device performance. The concept of self-hybridized exciton polaritons is not new, and does not seem to play a significant role in the device performance (actually it might introduce some intrinsic limits for the device performance), which has also been pointed out by the other reviewer. However, the polariton-enabled transport seems to be a quite interesting point, which is actually an important topic for the polaritonics [e.g., Nat Mater 2015, 14, 1123-1129]. Moreover, the polariton-mediated Purcell effect could be also some interesting point for boosting optoelectronic device performance, which might be related with this work [e.g., Nature 2024, 626, 300-306]. The authors are suggested to find some more significant points to support the claimed novelty. 2) For the tests of the strong coupling regime, there are still some points that should be carefully examined. First, the thickness-dependent coupling strength seems to be quite complicated. For the same cavity conditions, the coupling strength scales with the square-root of the thickness. For example, the thicknesses between 150-180 nm seem to host the similar l=2 cavity mode (Fig. R3.5a). In Table R3.2, the coupling strength for the thicknesses between 150 nm and 180 nm does not really follow this scaling law. This causes some confusion. Second, how did the authors determine the cavity linewidths? The linewidths are so broad and even broader than the exciton linewidths. For higher-order cavity modes, the linewidths generally should become narrower. The fitted cavity linewidths do not really follow this trend. Third, how did the authors determine the exciton linewidths. As the authors mentioned in the response, the oscillator strength of the excitons should become constant for the bulk thickness (the reference of Nature Photon 2015 is irrelevant with their argument there). For this scenario, the exciton linewidths should be also taken as a constant and independent of the bulk thickness. In Table R3.2, this does not seem to be the case. 3) In Fig. R3.8, some angle-resolved polariton branches of the experimental data are hard to be resolved for some thicknesses. For example, the upper branch for the thicknesses of 196 nm and 221 nm, and the lower branch for the thickness of 196 nm need to be resolved with better resolutions. 4) In Fig. R3.5c (the same in R3.9c, R3.13c), there are another extra reflectance dip at the exciton resonance. Does it correspond to the uncoupled exciton resonances? How does it affect the determination of the strong coupling regime here? 5) Why are there some thickness error bars for the samples in temperature-dependent measurements, while the thicknesses in the angle-resolved measurements seem to be very accurate without error bars? 6) We noted that in some figures of the angle-resolved spectra, the y-axis is labeled in "Energy". while it is also labeled in "Wavelength" in other spectra in the manuscript and supplementary materials. You are a senior editor at Nature Communications.

Read the paper and the peer-review interaction below. Based on the scientific concerns raised by the reviewers and the authors' point-by-point response, predict the editorial outcome.

Respond with EXACTLY one of these labels on the first line:
  major_revision
